VERIFY: dimensions with a text override in the DXF (user-typed measurement text) — believed upstream returns the GEOMETRIC value computed from definition points, ignoring the override text; pin this, it changes results on hand-edited drawings.

VERIFY per-dimension-type behavior (linear, aligned, angular, radius, diameter, ordinate): which types are supported at all, and the returned unit/interpretation for angular dimensions (degrees expected).

The DXF parser is the limited 2021.01 one: entities it cannot parse are skipped with warnings; splines are unsupported; files from modern CAD exports may parse partially — faithful compatibility includes those warnings.

Results are cached: repeated calls with identical (file, layer, name, origin, scale) do not re-read the file within a compile (performance surface; also means mid-compile file changes are not observed).
Missing arguments follow normal function-call rules (undef); calling with no file warns and returns undef (VERIFY).
scale multiplies the value AFTER extraction; origin participates only in coordinate-derived types (VERIFY).

This and dxf_cross are the only geometry-file-reading FUNCTIONS in the language — everything else file-related is a module; the reimplementation's expression evaluator therefore needs file-system access.
impl_notes: Decide support level early: (a) full clone — requires DIMENSION entity parsing in your DXF reader plus per-type value extraction (pin each type via oracle DXFs authored in LibreCAD/QCAD); or (b) stub — parse the call, warn ('dxf_dim not supported'), return undef; a stub keeps old scripts loadable but silently changes their geometry wherever the value fed dimensions, so document it loudly. Either way the function must exist in the function namespace (an unknown-function warning would differ from upstream). Probe set: one DXF containing every dimension type, a text-override dimension, a wrong-layer lookup, and a missing file.

name: dxf_cross
since: pre-2015.03 (legacy; still live and un-deprecated in 2021.01)
summary: Legacy DXF metadata reader FUNCTION, still live in 2021.01: finds a cross drawn as two intersecting LINE entities on a DXF layer and returns the [x, y] intersection point. Historically used to extract anchor/rotation points from 2D CAD drawings.

params.name: file
params.desc: Path to the DXF file, resolved relative to the including script.

params.name: layer
params.desc: DXF layer to search for exactly two LINE entities forming the cross; empty string for the default/all layers (VERIFY matching rule).

params.name: origin
params.desc: [x, y] applied when transforming the found point into model coordinates (VERIFY whether the point is returned as (p - origin) * scale or p * scale + origin — pin the direction).

params.name: scale
params.desc: Scale factor applied to the returned coordinates, default 1.

semantics: Parses the DXF (cached, same limited entity support as dxf_dim), collects the LINE entities on the requested layer, computes the intersection point of the two lines forming the cross, applies the origin/scale transform, and returns it as a 2-element vector [x, y]. Expression-level function; the classic idiom is translate(dxf_cross(...)) to anchor 3D features at a point marked in a 2D drawing.
edge_cases: Failure (missing file, no such layer, fewer or more than the expected two lines, or parallel lines with no intersection): returns undef with a WARNING of approximately 'WARNING: Can't find cross in 'file', layer 'layer'' (VERIFY exact text and each failure mode's behavior — especially >2 lines on the layer: believed first-two-found win or outright failure; pin it).
VERIFY: whether the two lines must literally intersect within their segments or are treated as infinite lines for the intersection computation.
Return type is a plain 2-vector usable directly in translate() (translate pads the missing z with 0).
Still live and not deprecation-warned in 2021.01 (VERIFY); removal in future releases is not part of the 2021.01 contract.
Same limited DXF parser and caching semantics as dxf_dim; unsupported entities skipped with warnings.
origin/scale transform direction must be pinned (see params) — an inverted convention silently shifts every anchored feature.
Calling with no file: warning + undef (VERIFY).
impl_notes: Same support decision as dxf_dim (full clone vs warn-and-undef stub); if cloning, author oracle DXFs with a two-line cross, a three-line layer, parallel lines, and non-touching segments to pin every failure branch and the origin/scale convention. The function must exist in the function namespace either way so scripts don't additionally trigger unknown-function warnings.

name: for (statement)
summary: Module-level loop: instantiates its body once per element of each iterable, binding the loop variable(s) immutably per iteration; all iteration results are implicitly unioned into one group.

params.name: varN = iterableN
params.desc: One or more comma-separated bindings. Iterable may be a vector (elements in order, heterogeneous allowed), a range [b:e]/[b:s:e] (expanded lazily, never materialized), a string (per code point), or a bare scalar/other value (single iteration with that value). Multiple bindings form NESTED loops over the cross product, first binding outermost — NOT parallel/zip iteration.

params.name: body
params.desc: A single child statement or a { } block. The block is a child scope; local assignments inside are allowed and invisible outside; multiple geometry statements inside one iteration are implicitly unioned.

semantics: Each iteration evaluates the body in a fresh child scope with the loop variable bound; the variable shadows any outer variable of the same name and cannot be mutated. The results of all iterations are collected under an implicit union (a group node), so 'for' inside difference() counts as ONE child. Ranges iterate begin, begin+step, ... while <= end (ascending) or >= end (descending for negative step) — endpoint inclusion follows the floating-point count, matching range semantics elsewhere. for is a statement, not an expression; there is no value-producing for outside list comprehensions. $-variables assigned in the body scope dynamically affect calls made within that iteration. Modifier characters (*,!,#,%) may prefix the whole for.
edge_cases: Multiple bindings in one for are a CROSS PRODUCT: for (a=[0,1], b=[0,1,2]) yields 6 iterations ordered a-major (a outer, b inner). Classic trap for users expecting zip.
Empty vector iterable: zero iterations, empty result, no warning.
Bare scalar (or boolean, undef, function value): exactly one iteration with the variable bound to that value — VERIFY: undef and other non-iterables all iterate once rather than zero times.

String iterable iterates one 1-character string per Unicode code point — VERIFY: version in which the for STATEMENT (as opposed to comprehensions) gained per-character string iteration; test for(c="abc") against the 2021.01 oracle.

Range with begin>end and implicit step 1: DEPRECATED legacy swap — iterates ascending anyway with a deprecation warning approx 'DEPRECATED: Using ranges of the form [begin:end] with begin value greater than the end value is deprecated' — VERIFY exact text; snapshots may instead treat it as empty.

Range step 0 (or a step whose element count explodes): warning approx 'WARNING: Bad range parameter in for statement: too many elements (N)' and the loop does not run — VERIFY exact text and the element-count threshold that triggers it.
Negative step with begin<end: zero iterations (empty), no warning — VERIFY.
Non-numeric range parts: warning + loop skipped — VERIFY message.
Loop variable is per-iteration immutable; assignments to it inside the body create a shadowing local for that block only.
The for body scope may contain module/function definitions; they are hoisted within that scope and redefined fresh per iteration.
Because iterations are implicitly unioned, intersection(){ for(...) ... } intersects one blob with nothing — this is why intersection_for exists.
for with zero children after modifier * is wholly ignored; ! inside a for body shows only the marked subtree of (VERIFY) the last-evaluated iteration — pin multi-! behavior against oracle.
Huge ranges are lazy: for(i=[0:1e6]) runs 1000001 iterations without allocating a vector; per-iteration module instantiation must hit the geometry cache for identical subtrees or real scripts crawl.
impl_notes: Pin against oracle: cross-product iteration order, scalar/undef single-iteration behavior, string iteration in statement form, all range warning texts, and the too-many-elements threshold. Implement ranges lazily. The implicit-union grouping must be a single CSG child (observable via difference/intersection).

name: intersection_for (statement)
summary: Identical header and iteration semantics to for, but the per-iteration results are INTERSECTED instead of unioned.

params.name: varN = iterableN
params.desc: Same forms as for: vector, range, string, scalar; multiple bindings = cross product, first binding outermost.

params.name: body
params.desc: Child statement or block; multiple statements within ONE iteration are still implicitly unioned with each other, then that per-iteration union participates in the overall intersection.

semantics: Evaluates the body once per iteration exactly like for, then combines the N per-iteration results with n-ary intersection. Exists because wrapping a plain for in intersection() is useless (the for's implicit union arrives as a single child). All iteration results must share dimensionality (mixing 2D and 3D is the standard boolean error).
edge_cases: Zero iterations (empty vector): empty result — VERIFY: whether identical to intersection() of nothing (empty geometry, no warning).
Exactly one iteration: result is that iteration's geometry unchanged (single-child intersection passes through).
Multiple statements inside one iteration's block are unioned first; only across iterations does intersection apply.
All range/scalar/string iterable quirks and warnings are shared verbatim with for — same deprecated reversed-range swap, same step-0 warning.
Mixing 2D and 3D results across iterations is an error: 'ERROR: Mixing 2D and 3D objects is not supported' — VERIFY exact text/position.
Disjoint per-iteration geometry yields empty result silently.
There is NO comprehension analogue — intersection_for is statement-level only.
intersection_for is a plain identifier-like keyword builtin, not reserved: VERIFY whether a user module named intersection_for can shadow it.
example: intersection_for (a = [0, 60, 120]) rotate([0, 0, a]) cube([12, 4, 4], center = true);
impl_notes: Share the entire iteration engine with for; only the combining node differs (union vs intersection). Probe empty-iteration and single-iteration cases against the oracle's .csg export.

name: if / else (statement)
summary: Module-level conditional instantiation: evaluates one branch's geometry/statements; 'else if' chains by nesting; branches are child scopes.

params.name: condition
params.desc: Any expression, tested with the standard truthiness rules (see truthiness entry).

params.name: then/else branch
params.desc: Single statement or { } block; each branch is its own child scope — assignments inside do NOT escape; multiple statements in a taken branch are implicitly unioned.

semantics: Only the taken branch is instantiated at all: the untaken branch produces no geometry, no echo output, no warnings, and no evaluation of its expressions. 'else if' is ordinary nesting (else followed by another if statement). The if statement as a whole is one child in its parent (so a modifier prefix applies to whichever branch runs). This is statement-level only; the expression-level conditional is the ternary ?:, and comprehensions have their own if clause.
edge_cases: Assignments inside a branch are scope-local: x=5; if(c){x=6;} leaves outer x==5 — the single most common user trap; must NOT be 'fixed'. VERIFY whether 2021.01 emits any shadow/unused warning here (believed: none).

Truthiness: false, 0, -0, "", [], undef are false; everything else true including "false", "0", [0], [[]], -1, inf, nan, ranges, function values — a nan condition takes the THEN branch. VERIFY ranges/function values truthy.
Condition expression errors (unknown variable etc.) warn and yield undef, which is falsy — evaluation continues with the else branch (if any).
if with no else and false condition contributes an empty group — VERIFY whether it appears as an empty group node or nothing at all in .csg output.
Dangling else binds to the nearest unmatched if, C-style.
Module/function definitions inside a branch are scoped to that branch's block only.
$-variable assignments inside a taken branch dynamically scope over calls within the branch only.
A modifier character may prefix the if itself (#if(c)...) and applies to the instantiated result — VERIFY oracle behavior.
There is no elif keyword; 'else if' is two tokens.
example: x = 3; if (x > 2) { cube(1); } else if (x > 0) sphere(1); else cylinder(1);
impl_notes: Guarantee the untaken branch is not evaluated (observable via echo/warnings). Reproduce branch scoping exactly; conditional values require the ternary, and scripts rely on inner assignment NOT leaking.

name: let (expression)
summary: Expression-level local bindings: evaluates bindings sequentially (each sees the previous), then evaluates the trailing expression in that extended scope; the whole thing is an expression.

params.name: nameN = exprN
params.desc: Sequential bindings; exprN may reference name1..name(N-1) and all outer-scope names. $-prefixed names allowed and become dynamically scoped for calls inside the body expression.

params.name: expression
params.desc: The result expression, evaluated with all bindings in scope.

semantics: Creates a new lexical scope shadowing outer names. Bindings are evaluated eagerly, strictly left to right, each binding visible to later ones — unlike top-level assignment there is NO last-write-wins reordering across let bindings; textual order is evaluation order. Usable anywhere an expression is allowed, including inside function bodies, default parameter values, and comprehension clause chains (see the comprehension let entry for clause form).
edge_cases: Repeating a name within one let (let(a=1, a=a+1) ...): the second binding sees the first and shadows it — VERIFY: whether a reassignment warning is emitted and whether the result is 2 (sequential) in 2021.01.
let(a=a) x binds a to the OUTER a (RHS evaluated before the new binding exists) — VERIFY: or undef-with-warning if no outer a.
Empty binding list let() expr: VERIFY whether it parses (believed legal, no-op).
Binding a $-variable (let($fn=64) f()) affects $-lookup dynamically in all calls made while evaluating the body expression.
let binds tighter than ?: — 'cond ? let(a=1) a : b' works; precedence/extent of the body expression is 'as far right as possible' — VERIFY grammar extent (let(...) a + b covers a+b).
Bindings are evaluated even if the body never uses them (eager, so their warnings/side echoes fire) — VERIFY eagerness with echo-expression inside a binding.
let does not create geometry scope — it is pure expression machinery; the statement form is a separate construct (2019.05).
example: echo(let (a = 2, b = a * 3) a + b); // ECHO: 8
impl_notes: Implement as nested environment frames; sequential visibility is load-bearing (differs from a scope's last-write-wins assignments). Pin duplicate-name-in-one-let behavior and grammar extent of the body against the oracle.

name: let (statement)
summary: Statement/module form of let (2019.05+): binds names sequentially in a new child scope over its child statement(s); the modern replacement for deprecated assign().

params.name: nameN = exprN
params.desc: Same sequential-binding rules as let-expression; $-variables allowed and dynamically scope over the subtree.

params.name: body
params.desc: Single child statement or { } block; children are implicitly unioned; the bindings are visible throughout.

semantics: Evaluates bindings left to right, each seeing earlier ones, then instantiates the child(ren) in that scope. The whole let statement is one child of its parent (implicit union of its own children). Unlike a { } block with plain assignments, let makes the sequential-binding intent explicit and, like all statement scopes, cannot mutate outer variables.
edge_cases: 2019.05+ only: on 2015.03 this is a syntax error — feature-test with version_num()>=20190500.
Bindings are sequential (let(a=1,b=a+1) sees a) — identical to expression form; VERIFY duplicate-name behavior matches expression form.
Plain assignments inside the child block coexist with let bindings; those block assignments follow normal last-write-wins within the block scope.
let-statement bindings shadow outer names for the subtree only; nothing leaks out.
$-bindings (let($fs=0.5){...}) affect all descendant instantiations and function calls dynamically.
Modifier characters may prefix the let statement and apply to its whole result.
VERIFY: let() with empty binding list as a statement parses.
Not to be confused with the comprehension let clause (expression context) — three syntactic homes total for let.
example: let (s = 4, h = s * 2) { cube([s, s, h]); }
impl_notes: Reuse the let-expression binding engine; wrap children in an implicit-union group node. Emit no deprecation (contrast assign).

name: assign (deprecated statement)
summary: Deprecated ancestor of the let statement: binds names in a child scope over its children; still parses and works in 2021.01 with a deprecation warning on every use.

params.name: nameN = exprN
params.desc: Bindings established for the child scope. VERIFY: whether bindings are sequential (each sees earlier ones, like let) or all evaluated in the outer scope — probe assign(a=1, b=a+1) against the oracle.

params.name: body
params.desc: Child statement or block; implicit union; bindings visible throughout.

semantics: Functionally the pre-2019.05 way to introduce per-scope bindings (historically the only way to 'change' a variable per iteration inside a for body). Emits a deprecation diagnostic each time it is instantiated, then behaves like a scoped binding construct. Never actually removed as of 2021.01; legacy Thingiverse-era scripts use it heavily.
edge_cases: Deprecation text approx: 'DEPRECATED: Assign is deprecated. Use a regular assignment instead.' — VERIFY exact wording, and that it is emitted per instantiation (so a loop over assign spams it; note GUI may rate-limit repeats).
VERIFY sequential vs simultaneous binding evaluation (assign(a=1,b=a+1)) — must be cloned exactly for legacy scripts.
$-variables may be bound via assign and dynamically scope like any binding — VERIFY.
assign is not a reserved word: VERIFY whether user code can define 'module assign()' and shadow it.
Under --hardwarnings: VERIFY whether the DEPRECATED diagnostic counts as fatal (deprecations vs warnings may be treated differently).
Children see the bindings exactly as with let; nothing leaks to the outer scope.
impl_notes: Keep it working forever (compat surface), emit the deprecation verbatim, and pin binding order with an oracle probe. Internally alias to the let-statement implementation once binding-order parity is confirmed.

name: variable assignment and scoping
summary: Assignment is declarative, not imperative: within one scope the LAST textual assignment to a name wins, taking effect at the position of the FIRST assignment; every { } block is a child scope that shadows rather than mutates.

params.name: name
params.desc: Identifier (letters/digits/underscore; $-prefixed names become dynamically scoped specials).

params.name: expression
params.desc: RHS evaluated once per scope evaluation, in dependency-free textual slot order.

semantics: A scope (file top level, module body, block, function body's parameter frame) collects its assignments; reassigning a name replaces the expression at the original slot, so a=1; b=a; a=2; gives b==2. Blocks (if/for/let/module bodies) are child scopes: an inner assignment shadows the outer name for that block and can never mutate the outer binding — conditional values must be written x = cond ? a : b. Variables are not hoisted the way module/function definitions are: an expression referencing a name defined only later in the SAME scope sees the (reordered) value per the slot rule, while a truly undefined name warns and yields undef.
edge_cases: Reassignment in one scope warns, approx 'WARNING: variable a was reassigned' — VERIFY exact 2021.01 text (and that the warning points at the later line).

The last-write-wins + first-slot rule is the mechanism that makes customizer/-D overrides (injected as TRAILING top-level assignments) override in-file values, and lets an including file override an include'd library's defaults regardless of textual order.
Referencing a never-assigned name: 'WARNING: Ignoring unknown variable ...' + undef — VERIFY text; is_undef(name) suppresses this warning (defined-guard idiom).
Inner-scope shadowing emits no warning in 2021.01 — VERIFY (some versions discussed a shadow warning).
Assignments interleave with geometry statements in a scope: pin against the oracle exactly when RHS evaluation happens relative to instantiations (echo ordering exposes it).
There are no compound assignments (+=, ++), no multiple-target assignment, and assignment is a statement only — never an expression.
Assigning a $-name at any scope makes it dynamically visible to the whole subtree/call-chain below.
Geometry is not assignable: x = cube(1); is a syntax error (instantiations are statements, not expressions).
example: a = 1; b = a; a = 2; echo(b); // ECHO: 2 (with a reassignment warning)
impl_notes: Implement scopes as ordered maps where reassignment replaces in place; evaluate slots in order. This rule is the foundation of include-override and -D semantics — golden-test it early. Warning texts are compat surface under --hardwarnings.

name: truthiness
signature: conversion of any value to boolean in if / ?: / && / || / assert / comprehension-if
summary: Exactly five falsy values — false, 0 (and -0), "", [], undef — everything else is true, including nan.

params.name: value
params.desc: Any OpenSCAD value: number, string, boolean, vector, range, undef, function value.

semantics: One shared truthiness table used by every conditional context: the if statement, comprehension if clause, ternary condition, logical operators (!, &&, ||), and assert's condition. Non-empty strings, non-empty vectors, all nonzero numbers (including negative, inf, and nan — the truthiness test is a plain != 0 comparison with no isnan special case, and nan != 0 is true under IEEE-754), ranges, and function values are true.
edge_cases: "false", "0", " " are TRUE (non-empty strings).
[0], [[]], [false], [undef] are TRUE (non-empty vectors).
-1, inf, -inf, and nan are all TRUE (nan != 0 holds under IEEE-754; there is no isnan carve-out in truthiness).
-0 is falsy (equals 0).
VERIFY: a range value (e.g. [0:0]) is truthy regardless of emptiness; VERIFY function values truthy.
nan is truthy yet is_num(nan) is false — the is_num carve-out is separate from truthiness; scripts probe both. So 0/0 ? a : b yields a.
undef arising from any warned type-mismatch propagates as falsy, silently steering else branches — the warning is the only trace.
impl_notes: Centralize one to_bool used by all six contexts; probe range/function-value truthiness once against the oracle.

name: iteration and control-flow model (absences)
signature: no while / break / continue / return / mutation
summary: The language has no imperative control flow whatsoever: all iteration is data-driven (for over iterables, comprehensions, recursion) and every function is a single expression.
semantics: There is no while loop, no break/continue, no return statement (a function's body IS its return expression), no goto, and no mutable variables. Early exit is expressed with the ternary; accumulation with recursion or C-style comprehension for; filtering with comprehension if. Any appearance of these keywords is simply an unknown identifier (they are not reserved).
edge_cases: while/break/continue/return are NOT reserved words: 'return = 1;' is a legal assignment and 'while(1)' parses as an unknown-module instantiation (warned and ignored) — VERIFY both.
Infinite loops are still reachable via non-terminating C-style comprehension for and via non-tail recursion (bounded by the recursion guard) — see recursion entry.
The absence of builtins for map/filter/fold/sort means recursion + comprehensions are the ecosystem's only tools; interpreter performance on those patterns is compatibility-critical.
example: function sum(v, i = 0) = i >= len(v) ? 0 : v[i] + sum(v, i + 1); echo(sum([1, 2, 3]));
impl_notes: Do not add extensions here; scripts feature-test versions, and a superset dialect breaks the compatibility contract. Ensure unknown-module handling covers 'while(...)' gracefully.

name: list comprehension
signature: [ clause-chain ]  where clause := for(...) | for(init;cond;update) | if(cond) [else] | let(...) | each expr | expr
summary: Vector-building expressions: inside a vector literal, generator clauses (for / C-style for / if / if-else / let / each) chain and nest arbitrarily, each chain terminating in an element expression; the result is always a vector.

params.name: clause-chain
params.desc: Any composition of the clause forms; each clause governs everything to its right until the chain terminates in an expression (or an each expr).

semantics: Clauses compose right-associatively: [for (x=v) if (p(x)) let (y=f(x)) each g(y)] iterates, filters, binds, and splices. Successive for clauses (or multiple bindings in one for) nest. The comprehension is an ordinary expression usable anywhere. Since 2019.05, generator clauses may be MIXED with plain literal elements inside one vector literal: [0, each v, for (i=r) i, 9] — plain elements contribute themselves in order, clauses contribute zero or more elements in place.
edge_cases: Empty productions collapse cleanly: [for (i=[]) i] is [], [if (false) 1] is [] — a comprehension may consist of a lone if clause with no for.

VERIFY: exact grammar corners of mixing literals with clauses in 2021.01 ([0, for(i=r) i] believed legal since 2019.05; pin whether a leading clause plus trailing literals, nested mixed literals, and trailing commas all parse).
A chain must end in exactly one element expression; parenthesize commas ([(a, b)] is a syntax error — no tuple expressions).
The element expression may itself be a vector literal containing further clauses (nesting builds nested vectors; use each to flatten one level).
Comprehensions over ranges expand element-by-element and DO materialize the result vector — [each [0:1e8]] is an OOM/time hazard by design.
Result vectors are heterogeneous-friendly; skipped if-clauses leave no hole (no undef padding).
String iteration in comprehension for yields 1-character strings: [for (c="ab") c] == ["a","b"].
Comprehension clauses exist ONLY inside [ ] vector literals — there is no generator expression outside brackets.
2015.03 baseline supports [for (...) expr] and let; each, C-style for, and if/else (the else part) require 2019.05.
impl_notes: Parse clauses as a right-nested tree inside vector literals; evaluation appends to one output buffer (must be O(1) amortized append). Golden-test the mixed literal/clause grammar matrix against the oracle before freezing the parser.

name: for (comprehension clause)
summary: Generator clause: iterates exactly like the for statement (vector/range/string/scalar; multi-binding = cross product) but produces list elements instead of geometry.

params.name: varN = iterableN
params.desc: Same iterable forms and cross-product multi-binding as the for statement; bindings scope over the rest of the clause chain.

params.name: rest
params.desc: The remainder of the clause chain (further clauses or the element expression), evaluated once per iteration.

semantics: For each element of the iterable(s), evaluates the rest of the chain with the variable(s) bound; each evaluation contributes its elements (one for a plain expression, zero-or-more through if/each) to the enclosing vector in iteration order. Order is deterministic: source order for vectors/strings, arithmetic order for ranges, a-major for cross products.
edge_cases: All range quirks are shared with the for statement: reversed-range deprecation swap, step-0 warning, lazy expansion — VERIFY the step-0 warning text in expression context ('in expression' vs 'in for statement').
Scalar iterable yields one iteration: [for (i=5) i] == [5]; VERIFY [for (i=undef) i] (believed [undef], one iteration).
Strings iterate per code point (1-char strings), non-ASCII safe.
[for (a=[1,2], b=[10,20]) a+b] == [11,21,12,22] — cross product a-major; NOT zip.
The loop variable shadows outer names for the chain only.
$-variables may be bound as loop variables? VERIFY: for ($x = v) — believed legal and dynamically scoped; probe.
Nested successive for clauses ([for (a=v) for (b=a) b]) are equivalent to multi-binding only when the inner iterable doesn't depend on the outer variable; dependence requires the nested spelling.
impl_notes: Share the iterable-expansion engine with the for statement verbatim so warning behavior stays identical; only the sink differs (list append vs child instantiation).

name: for (C-style comprehension clause)
signature: for (init1 [, init2...] ; condition ; update1 [, update2...]) element-producing-rest
summary: C-style generator (2019.05+), available ONLY inside comprehensions: initializes bindings, then repeatedly emits elements while the condition holds, applying the update assignments between iterations.

params.name: initN
params.desc: Comma-separated name=expr bindings evaluated once before the loop; VERIFY sequential visibility (init2 seeing init1), believed sequential like let.

params.name: condition
params.desc: Expression tested (standard truthiness) before EACH iteration including the first; false stops the loop.

params.name: updateN
params.desc: Comma-separated name=expr assignments producing the next iteration's bindings. All update RHS expressions are evaluated against the CURRENT iteration's values, then applied together (simultaneous update) — this is what makes the canonical Fibonacci example work. VERIFY simultaneity explicitly.

semantics: Bindings live in a clause-local scope covering condition, updates, and the rest of the chain. Loop: test condition; if truthy, evaluate the rest of the chain (contributing elements), then compute updates and repeat. Updates may introduce ONLY names already in the init list — VERIFY whether updating a name not initialized is legal. The statement-level for module has NO such form; using semicolons in a for statement header is a syntax error.
edge_cases: Canonical probe: [for (a=0, b=1; a<10; a=b, b=a+b) a] must yield [0,1,1,2,3,5,8] — sequential (new-a) updates would wrongly give [0,1,2,4,8]; clone the simultaneous-update semantics bug-for-bug. VERIFY against oracle.
Condition false initially: result contributes zero elements, no warning.

Non-terminating condition hangs the evaluator — VERIFY: believed NO built-in iteration cap in 2021.01 (unlike range element limits); decide whether to add an opt-in guard without changing default behavior.
Multiple updates and multiple inits are comma-separated; a trailing comma is a syntax error — VERIFY.

undef flowing into the condition is falsy and terminates the loop silently; nan is TRUTHY and does NOT terminate it — a condition that degrades to nan loops until another bound stops it (typical of arithmetic-warning cascades).
The clause composes like any other: [for (i=0; i<3; i=i+1) if (i!=1) i] == [0,2].
$-names as loop bindings: VERIFY legality/dynamic behavior.
2015.03 rejects this form with a syntax error — feature-test via version_num().
impl_notes: The Fibonacci probe is the single most important oracle test here — it pins update simultaneity. Also probe init sequentiality and updating-uninitialized-name behavior.

name: each
summary: Splice operator (2019.05+): inside a vector literal or comprehension chain, contributes the ELEMENTS of a vector or range (flattening one level) instead of the value itself; a non-iterable value contributes itself.

params.name: expression
params.desc: Value to splice: a vector contributes its elements in order; a range is expanded and contributes each numeric step; any other value (number, boolean, undef, function) contributes itself as a single element.

semantics: each is the one-level flatten/append primitive: [each [1,2], each [3:5]] == [1,2,3,4,5]. It is legal directly inside vector literals mixed with plain elements, and as the terminal producer of a comprehension chain ([for (r=rows) each r] flattens a matrix one level). each of a range is the idiomatic way to materialize a range into a vector.
edge_cases: each on a nested vector flattens exactly ONE level: [each [[1],[2]]] == [[1],[2]] spliced to [[1],[2]] — i.e. the inner vectors are the elements.

each on a string: VERIFY — believed to splice per-character in 2021.01 ([each "ab"] == ["a","b"]) but version coverage is uncertain; probe, since it differs from concat (which treats a string as a single element).
each on a scalar/boolean/undef yields that value as one element: [each 5] == [5], [each undef] == [undef] — VERIFY undef case.
each on an empty vector or empty range contributes nothing.
each expanding a range MATERIALIZES it — [each [0:1e9]] is a resource hazard; ranges elsewhere stay lazy.
each [b:e] with reversed bounds inherits the range's deprecation-swap behavior — VERIFY warning emission in this context.
each is only meaningful inside [ ] literals/comprehension chains; 'x = each v;' outside brackets is a syntax error.
each is a keyword (2019.05+): scripts using 'each' as an identifier break — part of the 2019.05 compat delta.
Chained clause form 'for (...) each expr' is the standard flatten idiom; 'if (c) each v' splices conditionally.
impl_notes: Implement as an element-sink adapter shared by literal and comprehension contexts. Probe string/undef splicing against the oracle before freezing; libraries use each heavily for concat-free appends.

name: if / if-else (comprehension clause)
summary: Filter/branch clause: without else, iterations failing the condition contribute nothing (filtering); with else (2019.05+), one of two productions is chosen per element.

params.name: condition
params.desc: Standard-truthiness expression, evaluated per surrounding iteration.

params.name: then/else production
params.desc: Rest-of-chain productions: a plain expression (one element), an each (splice), a let, a nested if, or a nested for.

semantics: Inside a chain, if guards everything to its right. The filter form is the only way to produce shorter-than-input lists from a single pass. Both arms may be full clause chains, so if (c) each a else each b and if (c) for (...) ... else ... compose. The untaken arm is not evaluated.
edge_cases: else requires 2019.05+; on 2015.03 only the filter form exists.
Dangling else binds to the nearest if within the chain — VERIFY with nested if/if/else probes.
A lone if with no for is legal: [if (c) 1] is [1] or [] — the conditional-element idiom.
Filtered-out iterations leave no placeholder (no undef).
VERIFY grammar corner: 'if (c) x else each y' and 'if (c) each x else y' both parse (mixed splice arms).
Condition sees all bindings from enclosing for/let clauses; undef conditions (e.g. from warned arithmetic) filter silently.
This clause is unrelated to the ternary; inside the ELEMENT expression itself you must use ?: (an if there is a syntax error).
impl_notes: Filter form is 2015.03, else form is 2019.05 — gate by reported version if you emulate old versions. Pin dangling-else association with oracle probes.

name: let (comprehension clause)
summary: Per-element bindings inside a comprehension chain: sequential let bindings scoped over the remainder of the chain.

params.name: nameN = exprN
params.desc: Sequential bindings (each sees earlier ones), re-evaluated once per surrounding iteration; may reference enclosing for/let bindings; $-names allowed.

params.name: rest
params.desc: Remainder of the clause chain evaluated with the bindings in scope.

semantics: Identical binding semantics to the let expression, positioned as a chain clause: [for (x=v) let (y = f(x), z = g(x,y)) if (z) y] computes intermediates once per element. Purely lexical; contributes no elements itself.
edge_cases: Bindings recompute every iteration — hoist loop-invariant work OUTSIDE the comprehension for performance; a compliant implementation must not observably cache (echo-expression in a binding fires per iteration).
Sequentiality matters: let (a=1, b=a+1) — b sees a; VERIFY duplicate-name behavior matches let-expression.
let directly before the element expression (no for) is legal: [let (a=1) a] == [1].
$-bindings here dynamically affect function calls in the rest of the chain.
Shadowing an enclosing loop variable is legal and scoped to the chain remainder.
impl_notes: Same environment machinery as let-expression; no special cases beyond chain plumbing.

name: module (definition and instantiation)
signature: module name(p1, p2 = default, ...) statement-or-{block}   /   name(args) [;| { children }]
summary: Defines a named, parameterized geometry producer; instantiation runs the body with matched arguments, implicitly unioning all geometry the body emits; call-site children are accessible via children().

params.name: name
params.desc: Identifier in the MODULE namespace (independent of function and variable namespaces).

params.name: p1, p2 = default
params.desc: Parameters; a parameter without a default that receives no argument binds undef (with a warning — VERIFY whether 2021.01 warns on missing non-defaulted args or binds silently). Defaults are expressions evaluated at call time and may reference EARLIER parameters and outer lexical scope.

params.name: body
params.desc: A block (or single statement) containing assignments, nested module/function definitions, and geometry statements; the body is a child scope; all emitted geometry is implicitly unioned.

semantics: Definitions are hoisted within their scope: a module may be instantiated textually before its definition. Nested definitions are lexically scoped to the enclosing body. Instantiation creates a fresh scope, binds parameters via the argument-matching rules, sets $children, pushes the module onto the instantiation stack (parent_module/$parent_modules), and evaluates the body. The call site may attach children with { } or a single trailing statement; children are lazily re-instantiated by each children() call, evaluating in the CALLER's lexical scope but under the CALLEE's current $-variable environment. Modules are not values: they cannot be assigned, passed, or returned (no module literals in any stable release).
edge_cases: Calling an undefined module: warning approx 'WARNING: Ignoring unknown module 'foo'' and the statement (including its children) is skipped — VERIFY text and that children are not evaluated.
Duplicate definition of the same module name in one scope: warning, last definition wins — VERIFY text (approx 'WARNING: module foo() was redefined').
User definitions SHADOW builtin modules (module cube() {...} hijacks cube) — VERIFY precedence; note the builtin becomes unreachable from inside (a self-call recurses).
Definitions are hoisted but their captured lexical environment is the whole scope (last-write-wins applies to variables they read).
A module body with zero geometry statements is legal and yields an empty group.

Passing children to a module that never calls children(): silently dropped, no warning in 2021.01 — VERIFY; but passing children to a builtin leaf primitive warns approx 'WARNING: module cube() does not support child modules' — VERIFY text and which builtins emit it.
Recursion is legal; depth-limited with 'ERROR: Recursion detected calling module 'name'' — see recursion entry.

Module names share the identifier lexicon; 'module for()' etc. are syntax errors only where the word is a reserved keyword (for, if, let, each, module, function, include, use, true, false, undef) — VERIFY the reserved set.
$-parameters may be declared as formals (module m($fn=8)) — VERIFY interaction: declared $-formal takes the passed value AND re-broadcasts dynamically to the subtree.
Semicolon after the closing brace of a definition is not required; an instantiation without children requires ';' or a child block.
example: module ring(r = 5) { difference() { circle(r); circle(r - 1); } } ring(8);
impl_notes: Model instantiation as tree-building only (no geometry values). Cache evaluated subtrees keyed by module+arguments+$-env — OpenSCAD's cache is why 1000x loops finish. Pin all warning texts and the shadowing precedence of builtins via oracle probes.

name: function (named definition)
summary: Defines a named function whose entire body is one expression; lives in the FUNCTION namespace, hoisted within its scope; recursion (with ternary as terminator) is the only looping construct.

params.name: name
params.desc: Identifier in the function namespace — may coexist with a module and a variable of the same name.

params.name: p1, p2 = default
params.desc: Same parameter semantics as modules: defaults evaluated at call time, may reference earlier parameters and outer scope; missing non-defaulted arguments bind undef.

params.name: expression
params.desc: The body and return value; a single expression (use let/ternary for structure). Terminated by ';'.

semantics: Callable before its textual definition (hoisting). Nested function definitions inside module bodies are lexically scoped. Calls evaluate arguments, bind via the standard matching rules, extend the definition's lexical environment, and evaluate the body; $-variables inside the body resolve DYNAMICALLY from the call site's $-environment. A named function is NOT a first-class value in 2021.01 — referring to 'name' as a variable hits the variable namespace instead (usually undef+warning); wrap it: g = function(x) name(x);.
edge_cases: Calling an undefined function: warning approx 'WARNING: Ignoring unknown function 'foo'' and the call yields undef; evaluation continues — VERIFY text.
Duplicate definition in one scope warns, last wins — VERIFY text.
User definitions shadow builtin functions (function sin(x) = 0;) — VERIFY precedence and whether any builtins are protected.
Ternary laziness is the recursion terminator; both && and || short-circuit only since 2019.05 — pre-2019.05-style guards relied solely on ?:.

Tail-call elimination since 2019.05: self- and mutual tail calls in ternary branches (and through let — VERIFY let-tail coverage) run to millions of iterations; non-tail recursion is depth-bounded with 'ERROR: Recursion detected calling function 'name'' — see recursion entry.
Arguments are evaluated eagerly, exactly once, left to right at the call site — VERIFY order observability via echo-expression arguments.
A function call in statement position is a syntax error (no expression statements); results must feed assignments, arguments, or conditions.
Function parameters and body form a child scope; body cannot see call-site locals (lexical capture of the DEFINITION site + dynamic $-env only).
echo()/assert() expression forms are the only tracing/validation tools inside a function body (2019.05+).
example: function fact(n) = n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); echo(fact(6)); // ECHO: 720
impl_notes: Keep the three namespaces strictly separate. TCE is mandatory for BOSL2-class libraries; implement the evaluator with an explicit heap stack (wasm shadow stacks are tiny). Pin unknown-function/duplicate-definition warning texts.

name: argument matching (calls to modules, functions, builtins)
signature: callee(pos1, pos2, ..., name1 = v1, name2 = v2, ..., $special = v, ...)
summary: Uniform call convention: positional arguments fill parameters in declaration order, named arguments bind by name in any order, unknown named arguments warn and are ignored — EXCEPT $-prefixed arguments, which are always accepted and injected into the callee's dynamic $-environment.

params.name: positional args
params.desc: Matched left-to-right to parameters not yet bound by name.

params.name: named args
params.desc: name=value pairs binding declared parameters in any order.

params.name: $-args
params.desc: Any $name=value is legal on ANY call without declaration; it does not need a matching parameter and becomes dynamically scoped for the callee's entire subtree/call chain (e.g. sphere(10, $fn=64)).

semantics: After matching, unbound parameters take their default expressions (evaluated in the callee's scope, earlier parameters visible); unbound parameters without defaults become undef. The same matcher serves user modules, user functions, function literals, and builtins — builtins additionally have their documented alternate spellings (r/d etc.) resolved on top of it.
edge_cases: Unknown named argument to a user module/function: warning approx 'WARNING: variable foo not specified as parameter' or 'Ignoring unknown parameter' — VERIFY exact 2021.01 text; the argument is discarded, the call proceeds.
Too many positional arguments: warning approx 'WARNING: Too many unnamed arguments supplied' — VERIFY text; extras discarded.
Same parameter bound twice (positionally and by name, or two named): later binding wins with a warning — VERIFY exact behavior/order and text; probe f(1, x=2) and f(x=1, x=2).
Positional arguments AFTER a named argument: VERIFY — believed to continue filling the next unbound positional slot (not an error); pin with probes, libraries accidentally rely on it.
Default expressions may reference earlier parameters (function f(a, b=a*2)) and outer lexical names; VERIFY referencing a LATER parameter (believed undef+warning).
Argument expressions are evaluated in the CALLER's scope before matching (eager), including for arguments that end up discarded — VERIFY discard-still-evaluated via echo probes.
$-args on builtins are the tessellation idiom; unknown PLAIN named args on builtins also warn-and-ignore (e.g. cube(size=1, bogus=2)) — VERIFY.
Declared $-formals (module m($fn=8)) both receive passed values and re-broadcast downward — VERIFY interplay when the caller also has $fn set.
example: module m(a, b = 10) { echo(a, b, $extra); } m(1, $extra = 99); // ECHO: 1, 10, 99
impl_notes: One shared matcher for everything; the warning set (unknown param, too many positional, duplicate) is --hardwarnings-fatal compat surface. Probe the named-then-positional corner and duplicate-binding precedence exhaustively against the oracle.

name: children
summary: Inside a module body, instantiates the child statements attached at the call site: all of them, a single 0-based index, a vector of indices, or a range of indices; each children() call re-instantiates (children can be stamped repeatedly under different transforms).

params.name: (none)
params.desc: children() with no argument instantiates all call-site children in order.

params.name: index
params.desc: 0-based single child index (number).

params.name: vector of indices
params.desc: children([0,2]) instantiates exactly those children, in the vector's order.

params.name: range
params.desc: children([0:2]) or [b:s:e]; each yielded index instantiates that child.

semantics: Children are passed lazily: the call-site block is not evaluated until a children() call instantiates it, and every children() call re-evaluates the selected children afresh. Children evaluate in the CALLER's lexical scope (they see the caller's variables, not the module's locals) but under the CALLEE's current dynamic $-environment (so a module can set $fn and its children see it). children() is only meaningful inside a module body; $children gives the count.
edge_cases: Out-of-range or negative index: warning approx 'WARNING: Children index (n) out of bounds (m children)' and that selection contributes nothing — VERIFY exact text and whether it is a warning or error.
Non-integer index: VERIFY (believed warning + skip); non-number argument: warning + skip.
children() with zero call-site children: no-op, no warning.
children([]) (empty vector) instantiates nothing.
Vector/range indices are each bounds-checked individually; a mixed valid/invalid vector instantiates the valid ones — VERIFY.
Multiple children() calls (or one inside a for) stamp the children multiple times — idiomatic; each stamping re-runs child evaluation (echo inside a child fires per stamping — VERIFY).
children() at top level / outside any module: error or warning — VERIFY text ('children() called outside module scope' approx).

Legacy child(i) still works in 2021.01 as a deprecated builtin: it instantiates the indexed child and emits 'DEPRECATED: child() will be removed in future releases. Use children() instead.' (removed only after 2021.01).
Scope rule probe: module m(){ x=99; children(); } x=1; m() echo(x); must print 1 (caller's lexical scope), while module m(){ $q=5; children(); } m() echo($q); prints 5 (callee's $-env).
Range index with reversed bounds inherits range deprecation-swap semantics — VERIFY in this position.
example: module twice() { children(0); translate([3, 0, 0]) children(0); } twice() cube(1);
impl_notes: Represent children as an unevaluated closure over (caller lexical scope, per-call $-env). The scope/$-env split is what BOSL2 depends on — golden-test both probes above. Pin the out-of-bounds diagnostic verbatim.

name: recursion limits and tail-call elimination
signature: recursive module instantiation / recursive function evaluation
summary: Both modules and functions may recurse; modules are hard-depth-limited with a 'Recursion detected' error; functions get tail-call elimination (2019.05+) so tail recursion runs to millions of frames while non-tail recursion is depth-bounded.
semantics: Module recursion (a module instantiating itself, directly or mutually) is legal and bounded by a fixed depth guard; exceeding it aborts evaluation with an error naming the module. Function recursion: since 2019.05 a self/mutual call in tail position (the selected branch of a ternary chain, and — VERIFY — through let bodies and the taken arm only) reuses the frame, so accumulator-style library code (BOSL2 etc.) runs 100k-1M+ deep. Non-tail function recursion hits a depth guard with an error naming the function. Evaluation halts on either error (like assert), with TRACE lines for the module stack.
edge_cases: Module error text approx: "ERROR: Recursion detected calling module 'name'" — VERIFY exact text and the depth limit (believed a fixed count on the order of low thousands; pin the observable number with a depth-probe script).
Function non-tail error approx: "ERROR: Recursion detected calling function 'name'" — VERIFY text and depth (probe function f(n)=n<=0?0:1+f(n-1); bisect the failing n).

TCE coverage: plain ternary tail calls definitely eliminated; VERIFY elimination through let(...) tail bodies, through echo()/assert() expression wrappers, and for mutual recursion between two functions.
A call under an operator (n * f(n-1)) is NOT a tail call — bounded; the same function rewritten with an accumulator is unbounded. Both behaviors are compatibility surface.
Function literals: VERIFY that TCE applies equally to recursive calls through variables holding function values.
Pre-2019.05: no TCE and no short-circuit &&/|| — only ?: laziness guarded recursion; irrelevant unless emulating old versions.
C-style comprehension for is iterative, not recursive — it does not consume recursion depth.
Errors here HALT evaluation (unlike warnings); under --hardwarnings nothing changes (already fatal).
example: function count(n, acc = 0) = n <= 0 ? acc : count(n - 1, acc + 1); echo(count(500000)); // needs TCE
impl_notes: Implement the evaluator iteratively (explicit heap stack / trampoline): wasm32 shadow stacks trap far below OpenSCAD's limits otherwise. Pin both depth limits and error texts via bisection probes; libraries genuinely rely on ~1M tail frames.

name: namespaces, hoisting, and shadowing
signature: modules, functions, and variables resolve in three independent namespaces per scope
summary: One identifier can simultaneously name a module, a function, and a variable; call syntax position (statement vs expression) selects the namespace; definitions are hoisted within their scope, duplicates warn with last-one-wins.
semantics: Statement-position name(...) resolves in the module namespace; expression-position name(...) resolves in the function namespace (in 2021.01, falling back to / interacting with variables holding function values — see calling-conventions entry); bare name resolves in the variable namespace. Each scope contributes to all three; lookup proceeds outward lexically. Module/function definitions are hoisted (usable textually before definition within the scope); variables follow the slot-reorder rule instead.
edge_cases: x = 1; function x(a) = a; module x() cube(); — all three coexist; echo(x) prints 1, echo(x(2)) prints 2, x(); makes a cube.
Duplicate module or function definition in one scope: warning, LAST definition wins (mirrors variable last-write-wins) — VERIFY warning text.
User definitions shadow builtins in both callable namespaces — VERIFY precedence for e.g. 'module cube()' and 'function sin()'; also VERIFY whether ANY builtins are un-shadowable.

Inner-scope definitions shadow outer ones lexically; include<> merges definitions into the including scope (subject to duplicate-warn/last-wins), use<> populates only the two callable namespaces of the using file's top scope.
Hoisting + lexical capture: a hoisted function reading a scope variable sees the slot-reordered final value, even if the call textually precedes the assignment.

Keywords (module, function, if, else, for, let, each, echo, assert, include, use, true, false, undef) cannot be identifiers in ANY namespace — echo and assert joined the reserved set with their 2019.05 expression forms and are NOT shadowable in 2021.01; other builtin names (version, intersection_for, cube, sin, ...) are ordinary identifiers and shadowable.
example: x = 1; function x(n) = n * 10; module x() sphere(1); echo(x, x(2)); x();
impl_notes: Three maps per scope frame. The statement/expression position rule does all disambiguation — no unified symbol table. Probe builtin shadowing and the reserved-word list against the oracle parser.

name: function literal
summary: Anonymous first-class function value (NEW in 2021.01): an expression producing a callable closure; supports default parameters; captures its lexical environment; $-variables inside the body still resolve dynamically at call time.

params.name: p1, p2 = default
params.desc: Parameter list with the same syntax and matching rules as named functions (positional/named/$-args, defaults referencing earlier parameters).

params.name: expression
params.desc: Body expression evaluated on call in the captured definition environment extended with the arguments.

semantics: Evaluating the literal yields a value of the distinct 'function' type: storable in variables and vectors, passable as arguments, returnable from functions — enabling user-space map/filter/fold (there are no builtins for those). The closure captures the lexical scope at the definition site; since bindings are immutable, capture-by-environment and capture-by-value are indistinguishable EXCEPT for $-variables, which are looked up dynamically in the CALLER's $-environment at each call, not the definition's.
edge_cases: A named 'function f(x) = ...' is NOT automatically a value: is_function(f) sees the VARIABLE f (usually undef + unknown-variable warning); the idiom is g = function(x) f(x); — no bare function references exist in 2021.01.

Self-recursion through the storing variable works: fac = function(n) n <= 0 ? 1 : n * fac(n - 1); — the body looks up 'fac' at call time in the captured scope where the slot exists — VERIFY this works in 2021.01 including under the assignment-slot-reordering rule.

echo of a function value prints a source-like rendering approx 'function(x, y = 1) ...' — VERIFY exact text (parameter list formatting, whether the body prints); str() of a function value follows the same rendering — VERIFY.
$-dynamic probe: f = function() $q; module m() { $q = 5; echo(f()); } m(); prints 5 — the definition site had no $q. Clone exactly; BOSL2 callbacks depend on it.

Function values in operators: f + 1, f == g, f < g — VERIFY (believed undef for arithmetic/relational; == on functions believed false unless — VERIFY — identical value); function values are truthy — VERIFY.
Function type is distinct: is_function true, is_num/is_list/is_string/is_bool false; len(f) undef; f[0] undef.

Literals appear anywhere expressions do: in vectors [function(x) x], as defaults (function g(h = function(x) x) = h(1)), in ternaries; precedence: the body extends maximally right — parenthesize when embedding, e.g. (function(x) x + 1)(2) — VERIFY grammar extent.

On 2019.05 and earlier the literal syntax is a hard SYNTAX ERROR (file fails to parse entirely) — feature-gate whole files, not call sites; libraries isolate 2021.01 code in separate files for this reason.
Default parameter expressions are evaluated at CALL time in the closure environment (earlier params visible) — same rules as named functions.
VERIFY: tail-call elimination applies to recursive calls through function-value variables (believed yes).
example: add = function (a, b = 1) a + b; echo(add(2), add(2, 5)); // ECHO: 3, 7
impl_notes: Represent as closure {param list, body AST, captured env ref}; $-lookup must bypass the captured env and use the caller's dynamic chain. Pin the echo rendering text and the equality/ordering behavior of function values via oracle probes — user code pattern-matches echo output in tests.

name: is_function
summary: Type predicate (2021.01): true iff the argument is a function value (a function literal / closure); false for every other type.

params.name: value
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Returns true only for values of the function type introduced in 2021.01. Completes the is_* family (is_undef/is_num/is_bool/is_string/is_list from 2019.05). Never warns, never errors, total over all values.
edge_cases: is_function(f) where f is a NAMED function definition: resolves f in the VARIABLE namespace — typically 'unknown variable' warning + undef + result false; named definitions are not values.
is_function on undef/numbers/strings/vectors/ranges/booleans: false, silently.
is_function is itself a builtin FUNCTION, not a keyword — VERIFY shadowability by a user definition.
On 2019.05: is_function does not exist — calling it warns unknown-function and yields undef (falsy), so naive feature probes accidentally 'work'; version_num() >= 20210100 is the reliable gate.
VERIFY: is_function(is_function) — the bare name again hits the variable namespace (undef + warning + false), NOT true.
example: f = function (x) x * 2; echo(is_function(f), is_function(5)); // ECHO: true, false
impl_notes: Trivial type-tag check; the interesting compat surface is the variable-namespace lookup of the argument (warnings included).

name: function-value calling conventions
signature: callee-expression(args)  — callee may be any expression yielding a function value
summary: Call syntax generalizes in 2021.01: any postfix-position expression that evaluates to a function value is callable — variables, parenthesized expressions, vector elements, and results of other calls (currying/chaining).

params.name: callee-expression
params.desc: Identifier, (expr), v[i], v.x, or f(...) — anything in postfix/primary position.

params.name: args
params.desc: Matched to the function value's parameters with the standard rules (positional, named, defaults, $-injection).

semantics: For a call name(args) with an IDENTIFIER callee, 2021.01 must resolve between the function namespace (named definitions) and the variable namespace (function values). For non-identifier callees ((expr)(x), list[i](x), f(x)(y)) only the value path exists. Arguments are evaluated eagerly in the caller's scope; the body runs in the closure's captured environment; $-variables flow from the caller's dynamic environment.
edge_cases: VERIFY resolution precedence when BOTH 'function f(x) = 1;' and 'f = function(x) 2;' exist in scope: pin which one f(0) calls in 2021.01 (believed: a local variable holding a function takes precedence over an outer named function, and — VERIFY — a same-scope named function beats the variable; probe all scope combinations against the oracle and clone exactly).

Calling a non-function value: v = 5; v(1) — warning approx 'WARNING: Can't call function on number' (or unknown-function if no variable matches) and the call yields undef — VERIFY exact text per type (undef callee, string callee, vector callee).
Chained/curried calls work: adder = function(a) function(b) a + b; echo(adder(2)(3)); // 5 — inner literal captures a.
Vector-of-functions dispatch: fs = [function(x) x, function(x) -x]; fs[1](3) == -3.
Named and $-arguments work on function values exactly as on named functions, including unknown-named-arg warnings — VERIFY warning text parity.
A call is still not a statement: 'f(1);' at statement level parses as a MODULE instantiation of f (module namespace), not a function-value call — the two worlds never mix.
VERIFY: member-access callee (obj.x(args)) — .x is vector swizzle in 2021.01, so v.x(1) calls the function stored as the first vector element.
example: compose = function (f, g) function (x) f(g(x)); inc = function (x) x + 1; echo(compose(inc, inc)(5)); // ECHO: 7
impl_notes: Grammar change: postfix call must accept any primary expression, while statement-level instantiation stays module-namespace-only. The identifier-callee precedence question is THE oracle probe to run first — libraries with shadowed helper names depend on whichever answer 2021.01 gives.

name: number literals
summary: Numeric literals; all numbers are IEEE-754 double precision. There is no integer type.
semantics: Decimal digits with optional fraction and optional e/E exponent (exponent sign optional). A leading '.' form (.5) is accepted. Every number in the language is a C double; integer-looking values are doubles that happen to be integral. Literal value is the nearest double (standard strtod rounding).
edge_cases: No hex, octal, or binary literals - '0x10' is a parse error/lexes as 0 followed by identifier x10 (VERIFY: exact lexer behavior on 0x10).
No literal for inf or nan; they arise only from arithmetic (1/0, 0/0) - the identifiers 'inf'/'nan' are ordinary undefined variables.
Literals exceeding double range (1e999) become inf silently (strtod overflow).
VERIFY: trailing-dot form '5.' accepted by the lexer.
Negative numbers are unary minus applied to a positive literal, not part of the literal - matters for precedence with ^.
-0 exists as a distinct double but echo prints it as 0 (UNIQUE_ZERO in 2021.01's double-conversion formatter); its sign is observable only via arithmetic such as 1/-0 == -inf.
impl_notes: Parse with strtod-equivalent; store f64 everywhere. Pin 0x, 5., and 1e999 behavior via oracle probes.

name: string literals
summary: Double-quoted UTF-8 string literals with a small escape set.
semantics: Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode code points stored as UTF-8. Only double quotes delimit strings. Recognized escapes: \" \\ \t \n \r, plus (since 2015.03) \x## (two hex digits, one byte), \u#### (4 hex digits) and \U###### (6 hex digits) for Unicode code points. Arbitrary UTF-8 (including astral characters) may appear directly in source.
edge_cases: Unicode/hex escapes \x## (hex byte), \u#### and \U###### (code points) are supported since 2015.03. VERIFY: behavior for invalid hex digits and out-of-range \U values — pin against oracle.
VERIFY: unrecognized escape like \q - believed to keep the character (or backslash+char); pin against oracle.
No single-quoted strings; ' is a syntax error.
Unterminated string at EOF is a parse error.
A literal newline inside the quotes: VERIFY whether accepted verbatim or an error.
len/indexing count code points, not bytes; s[i] yields a 1-character string.
impl_notes: Store UTF-8, index by code point. Oracle-probe unknown escapes and embedded newlines before freezing the lexer.

name: boolean and undef literals
summary: Keyword literals for the two booleans and the undefined value.
semantics: true/false are the boolean type; undef is a distinct singleton type meaning 'no value'. undef is what missing parameters, failed lookups, out-of-range indexing, and type-mismatched operations produce.
edge_cases: true == 1 is false: no numeric coercion in ==; but both true and 1 are truthy in conditions.
undef == undef is true; undef compared relationally (<) is undef.
Operations on undef (undef+1 etc.) yield undef with a console WARNING; evaluation continues.
Bare use of a never-assigned variable warns ('WARNING: Ignoring unknown variable ...' - VERIFY exact text) and yields undef; is_undef(var) suppresses that warning.
They are keywords: 'true = 5;' is a syntax error.
example: echo(true, false, undef, true==1); // ECHO: true, false, undef, false

name: vector literals
summary: Bracketed, comma-separated, heterogeneous, arbitrarily nested list values - the only container type.
semantics: Evaluates each element expression left to right and produces a vector. Elements may be any mix of types including vectors (matrices are vectors of row vectors). [] is the empty vector. Inside a vector literal, generator clauses are also legal: 'each expr' splices, 'for(...) expr', 'if(...)...', and 'let(...) expr' comprehension clauses may be mixed with plain elements in 2021.01.
edge_cases: Trailing comma [1,2,] is tolerated (VERIFY: version that introduced tolerance; believed accepted in 2021.01).
[1, each [2,3], for(i=[4:5]) i] is legal 2021.01 and yields [1,2,3,4,5] (VERIFY grammar corners).
each on a range expands it; each on a non-list yields the value itself as one element.
[a:b] with a colon is a RANGE literal, not a 2-vector - the bracket syntax is overloaded.
Vectors compare with == deeply; there is no reference identity.
Comprehension result is always a fresh vector; empty generator yields [].
impl_notes: Comprehension clauses inside plain literals share one grammar; implement the vector literal as a list of element-producers.

name: comments and lexical structure
summary: C-style comments; whitespace-insensitive token stream; identifier and keyword rules.
semantics: // comments run to end of line; /* */ block comments do NOT nest. Identifiers are [A-Za-z0-9_]+ not starting with a digit; the $ prefix creates special (dynamically scoped) variable names. Keywords: module, function, if, else, for, let, each, echo, assert, include, use, true, false, undef — echo and assert are lexer keywords since their 2019.05 expression forms ('echo = 5;' and 'module echo() ...' are parse errors), though both remain callable in statement position via a dedicated module-name grammar production (alongside for/let/each). intersection_for and other builtins are ordinary identifiers, not keywords.
edge_cases: /* /* */ ends at the FIRST */ - non-nesting block comments.
include <file> and use <file> use angle brackets with a raw path (spaces allowed inside); they are directives, not expressions.
Customizer metadata lives in comments, so a compatible implementation must retain or re-scan comments.
$ alone is not an identifier; $foo is valid anywhere an identifier is, and any $name may be invented by users.
Identifiers are case-sensitive; there is no reserved 'in' or 'return'.
No semicolon after a { } block; assignment statements and instantiations require ';'.

name: operator precedence
summary: Full expression-operator precedence and associativity table.
semantics: Highest to lowest: 1) postfix function call f(x), indexing v[i], member v.x; 2) ^ exponentiation (right-associative, 2021.01); 3) unary !, -, + ; 4) * / % (left-assoc); 5) binary + - (left-assoc); 6) relational < <= >= > (left-assoc, non-chaining semantically); 7) == != (left-assoc); 8) && ; 9) || ; 10) ternary c?a:b (right-associative, lazy). Parentheses group. Assignment is a statement, not an expression.
edge_cases: ^ binds tighter than unary minus: -2^2 == -4 (VERIFY: this exact corner against oracle; grammar places unary below ^).
2^-3 parses (unary minus in the exponent operand) and yields 0.125.
x^y^z == x^(y^z) (right-assoc).
a==b==c parses as (a==b)==c - comparing a boolean to c, usually false; no chained comparisons.
-x[0] is -(x[0]); !f(x) is !(f(x)) - postfix beats unary.
a?b:c?d:e == a?b:(c?d:e).
Calling a non-function value: WARNING and undef (VERIFY text, e.g. 'WARNING: Can't call function on ...').
let(...) expr, echo(...) expr, assert(...) expr, function(...) expr are prefix expression forms that extend to the right with the lowest precedence.
impl_notes: since reflects the last material change (^ insertion). Encode the table in a Pratt parser and oracle-probe -2^2, 2^3^2, -x%y.

name: binary + and -
summary: Numeric addition/subtraction and recursive elementwise vector addition/subtraction; no broadcasting.

params.name: a
params.desc: Number, or vector (recursively numeric/vector) matching b's shape.

params.name: b
params.desc: Same shape as a.

semantics: number+number is IEEE addition. vector+vector of EQUAL length adds elementwise, recursing into nested vectors (so matrix+matrix works). Everything else is undef with a WARNING.
edge_cases: scalar+vector, vector+scalar: undef with WARNING - there is NO broadcasting for +/-.
Unequal-length vectors: undef with WARNING (VERIFY: some historic versions truncated to the shorter; 2021.01 believed undef).
"a"+"b" is undef with WARNING - str() is the only concatenation.
true+1, undef+1: undef with WARNING; approximate text 'WARNING: undefined operation (bool + number)' (VERIFY exact wording/format).
inf and nan propagate per IEEE: inf+(-inf)=nan, no extra warning.
Nested mismatch ([1,[2]]+[1,2]) makes only the mismatched element undef or the whole result undef - VERIFY which; believed whole-result undef.
Warnings count toward --hardwarnings fatality.
impl_notes: Oracle-probe unequal lengths and nested mismatches; the warning text is compatibility surface.

name: * multiplication
summary: Shape-dispatched: scalar product, scalar-vector scaling, vector dot product, and matrix products.

params.name: a
params.desc: Number, vector, or matrix (vector of equal-length numeric row vectors).

params.name: b
params.desc: Number, vector, or matrix conforming to a.

semantics: Dispatch by operand shapes: num*num -> num; num*vector or vector*num -> elementwise scale (recursive, so num*matrix scales every entry); vector*vector -> DOT PRODUCT (scalar; equal lengths required); matrix*vector -> vector (rows dot v); vector*matrix -> vector (v dot columns); matrix*matrix -> matrix product. Matrices are row-major nested lists.
edge_cases: vector*vector returning a scalar is the classic trap - elementwise multiply does not exist; users write comprehensions.
Length/dimension mismatch: undef with WARNING (VERIFY text).
Ragged 'matrices' (rows of unequal length): undef/WARNING - VERIFY exact behavior.
bool*num, string*num: undef with WARNING.
Empty vectors: []*[] -> 0 (empty dot product) - VERIFY; matrix forms with empty dims - VERIFY.
Mixed content vectors ([1,"a"]*[1,2]): undef with WARNING.
No implicit transpose anywhere; v*m treats v as a row vector.
impl_notes: Pin dispatch order and every mismatch case via oracle; BOSL2 leans on all matrix forms.

name: / division
summary: Numeric division; vector/scalar divides elementwise; division by zero yields inf/nan with a warning.

params.name: a
params.desc: Number or (recursively numeric) vector.

params.name: b
params.desc: Number divisor.

semantics: num/num is IEEE division. vector/num divides each element, and num/vector divides the scalar by each element (both recursive into nested vectors, so matrix/scalar works and 10/[2,5] yields [5,2]). vector/vector and non-numeric shapes are undef with WARNING.
edge_cases: 1/0 -> inf, -1/0 -> -inf, each with 'WARNING: division by zero' (VERIFY exact text/format).
0/0 -> nan with the same division-by-zero WARNING (VERIFY whether warning fires for 0/0).
scalar/vector IS supported elementwise: 10/[2,5] == [5,2], recursing into nested vectors; only vector/vector division (and non-numeric operands) is undef with WARNING.
vector/vector: undef with WARNING (no elementwise divide).
[1,2]/0 -> [inf, inf] plus warning(s) - VERIFY warning count (per element vs once).
-0 results follow IEEE (1/-0 -> -inf).

name: % modulo
summary: Floating-point remainder with C fmod semantics; result sign follows the dividend.

params.name: a
params.desc: Dividend (number).

params.name: b
params.desc: Divisor (number).

semantics: Computes fmod(a,b): the remainder of truncating division; result has the sign of a (or is zero). Works on fractional operands: 5.5 % 2 == 1.5. Numbers only.
edge_cases: -7 % 3 == -1 and 7 % -3 == 1 (sign follows dividend) - NOT Python's floored modulo; libraries implement positive mod themselves.
x % 0 -> nan; VERIFY whether the division-by-zero WARNING is emitted for %.
inf % x -> nan; x % inf -> x (fmod semantics).
vector % anything: undef with WARNING.
Non-numeric operands: undef with WARNING.
There is no integer division; users write floor(a/b).

name: ^ exponentiation
summary: Power operator, new in 2021.01; right-associative; identical math to pow().

params.name: base
params.desc: Number.

params.name: exponent
params.desc: Number.

semantics: Computes C pow(base, exponent). Right-associative: a^b^c == a^(b^c). Binds tighter than unary minus but looser than postfix call/index. Numbers only.
edge_cases: -2^2 == -4 (unary minus applied after ^) - VERIFY this precedence corner against oracle.
0^0 == 1 (C pow convention).
(-8)^(1/3) -> nan (pow of negative base with non-integer exponent); (-8)^2 == 64.
0^-1 -> inf; VERIFY whether a warning accompanies it (believed none - pure pow).
Non-numeric operand: undef with WARNING.
Scripts targeting <=2019.05 must use pow(); ^ is a syntax error there - a compat-mode consideration.
1^inf == 1, x^0 == 1 even for x=nan? pow(nan,0)==1 per C - VERIFY OpenSCAD matches.
impl_notes: Route ^ and pow() through the same pow implementation so they can never diverge.

name: unary minus and plus
summary: Numeric negation; -vector negates elementwise recursively.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number or recursively numeric vector.

semantics: -number negates; -vector negates every element recursively (so -matrix works). Precedence: below ^, above * / %.
edge_cases: -true, -"a", -undef: undef with WARNING.
-[1,"a"]: VERIFY - believed undef (or element-undef) with WARNING.
-0 is produced and is IEEE negative zero; echo display of -0 must be pinned (VERIFY).
Unary + : VERIFY whether the grammar accepts +x at all in 2021.01 (believed accepted as a no-op on numbers); pin it.
--x parses as -(-x) (two unary operators).
-2^2 is -(2^2) - see precedence.

name: ! logical not
summary: Truthiness negation; always returns a boolean.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value, judged by truthiness.

semantics: Returns true if x is falsy, false if truthy. Falsy values: false, 0 (and -0), "", [], undef — five values; nan is truthy, so !(0/0) is false. Everything else is truthy, including "false", "0", [0], [[]], negative numbers, ranges, and function values.
edge_cases: !undef == true; !(0/0) == false (nan is truthy — the truthiness test is a plain != 0) — no warning for either.
!"false" == false (non-empty string is truthy).
![] == true but ![[]] == false.
!range: a range is truthy (VERIFY: including degenerate ranges).
Never yields undef; output is strictly boolean.
example: echo(!0, !"", ![0], !undef); // ECHO: true, true, false, true

name: && and || logical and/or
summary: Short-circuiting (since 2019.05) logical operators returning booleans, not operands.

params.name: a
params.desc: Left operand, judged by truthiness.

params.name: b
params.desc: Right operand, evaluated only if needed (2019.05+).

semantics: a && b: if a is falsy, result is false WITHOUT evaluating b; else result is the truthiness of b as a boolean. a || b: if a is truthy, result is true without evaluating b; else truthiness of b. Both return true/false, never the operand value (unlike JS/Python).
edge_cases: Short-circuit only since 2019.05; in 2015.03 both sides were always evaluated - recursion guards like 'i<len(v) && v[i]>0' rely on the 2019.05 behavior.
Return value is boolean: (5 && 7) == true, not 7 (VERIFY per seed).
undef && anything == false, no warning from the && itself.
Side effects in the skipped operand (echo-expression, assert-expression) do not fire - observable laziness.
&& binds tighter than ||: a || b && c == a || (b && c).
No 'and'/'or' keywords; no xor operator.
example: echo(true || assert(false) 1); // ECHO: true (assert never evaluated)
impl_notes: Laziness must extend through assert/echo expression operands; pin the boolean-not-operand return with echo(1&&2).

name: ?: ternary conditional
summary: Lazy conditional expression - the language's only recursion terminator.

params.name: cond
params.desc: Any value, judged by truthiness.

params.name: then_expr
params.desc: Evaluated only when cond is truthy.

params.name: else_expr
params.desc: Evaluated only when cond is falsy.

semantics: Evaluates cond; evaluates and returns exactly one branch. The untaken branch is NEVER evaluated - this laziness is what allows recursive functions to terminate. Right-associative; lowest precedence.
edge_cases: An eager implementation infinite-loops every recursive library function - laziness is non-negotiable.
A cond of undef takes the else branch (falsy); a cond of nan takes the THEN branch (nan is truthy in 2021.01); no warning for either.
Nesting chains right: a?b:c?d:e == a?b:(c?d:e); there is no 'elif'.
A ternary in tail position is eligible for tail-call elimination (2019.05+) - both branches are tail contexts.
No warning ever originates from ?: itself; warnings come from the evaluated branch only.
example: function fact(n) = n<=1 ? 1 : n*fact(n-1); echo(fact(10)); // ECHO: 3.6288e+6

name: == and != equality
summary: Total, deep, structural equality across all types; mismatched types are simply unequal (false, not undef).

params.name: a
params.desc: Any value.

params.name: b
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Returns true/false for any operand pair. Numbers compare by IEEE ==; strings by exact code-point sequence; booleans by identity; vectors recursively (length then elementwise); undef==undef is true. Values of different types are unequal. != is the exact negation.
edge_cases: nan == nan is false and nan != nan is true (even to itself); a vector containing nan is therefore never == to anything, including itself (VERIFY the vector-with-nan case).
true == 1 is false; "1" == 1 is false - zero coercion.
0 == -0 is true (IEEE).
[1,2] == [1,2,3] is false; [] == [] is true; deep nesting compares fully.
Range equality: [1:2]==[1:2] - VERIFY (believed true via begin/step/end compare); range == list is false.
Function-literal equality (2021.01): VERIFY behavior (believed false/undef for distinct literals) - pin against oracle.
Never emits a warning; never returns undef (contrast with relational operators).
impl_notes: Two different comparison regimes coexist (== total, < partial); do not unify them.

name: < <= >= > relational
signature: a < b, a <= b, a >= b, a > b
