summary: Partial ordering defined ONLY for number-number and string-string; everything else yields undef.

params.name: a
params.desc: Number or string.

params.name: b
params.desc: Same type as a.

semantics: Numbers compare by IEEE ordering. Strings compare lexicographically by Unicode code point (no locale, no normalization). Any other combination - vectors, booleans, undef, ranges, functions, or mixed number/string - yields undef, with a WARNING (VERIFY: warning presence/text for each mismatch).
edge_cases: Comparisons involving nan are false (IEEE), not undef: nan<1, nan>=1 both false - VERIFY OpenSCAD matches C here rather than returning undef.
"Z" < "a" is true (code points 90 < 97); "abc" < "abd"; prefix < longer ("ab" < "abc").
[1] < [2] is undef - vectors are NOT ordered; a ternary on it takes the else branch.
true < false: undef (booleans unordered) - VERIFY.
undef in a comparison propagates undef; combined with ?: this silently takes else branches - a classic silent-bug source to reproduce faithfully.
-0 < 0 is false (they are equal).

name: v[i] indexing
summary: Zero-based element access on vectors and strings; anything invalid yields undef.

params.name: value
params.desc: Vector or string.

params.name: index
params.desc: Number; must be an integral value in [0, len).

semantics: vector[i] returns the i-th element. string[i] returns the i-th code point as a 1-character string. Chains for matrices: m[1][2]. Index must be a non-negative integer-valued number within bounds; everything else returns undef.
edge_cases: No negative indexing (v[-1] is undef, not last element) and no slicing.
Non-integer index (v[1.5]) -> undef; integral doubles (v[1.0], v[2/2]) work.
Out of range -> undef; VERIFY whether a warning accompanies out-of-range string/vector indexing (believed silent undef in expressions).
Indexing a range, number, boolean, or undef -> undef (VERIFY warning).
String indexing is by code point over UTF-8 - byte indexing corrupts non-ASCII.
v[true] -> undef (no bool-to-number coercion) - VERIFY.
v["x"]: undef - member-style access via brackets does not exist; use v.x.

name: .x .y .z member access
summary: Swizzle sugar for the first three vector elements; 2019.05+.

params.name: vector
params.desc: A vector value; .x/.y/.z read elements 0/1/2.

semantics: v.x == v[0], v.y == v[1], v.z == v[2]. Works on any vector, including nested access like m[1].z. Read-only (no assignment targets).
edge_cases: Only x, y, z are supported in 2021.01; v.w or v.foo - VERIFY: believed a parse-time or eval-time error rather than undef; pin exact behavior/message.
Short vector: [1].y -> undef (out of range).
On non-vectors (string, number, range, undef): undef, VERIFY warning.
Snapshot 'object' values (textmetrics) extend dot access to arbitrary keys - snapshot-only.
Pre-2019.05 scripts cannot use it; feature-test via version_num()>=20190500.

name: function call operator
summary: Invokes a named function/builtin or (2021.01) any expression evaluating to a function value.

params.name: callee
params.desc: Function name, or any postfix expression yielding a function value (2021.01).

params.name: arguments
params.desc: Positional first, then named in any order; $-named arguments always accepted and become dynamic specials for the call.

semantics: Arguments bind positionally then by name; a parameter given twice - VERIFY (warning, later wins?). Missing parameters without defaults become undef. Unknown named arguments WARN and are ignored, except $-prefixed ones which are always accepted. Defaults may reference earlier parameters. Expression-callees like funcs[i](x) or (pick(n))(x) are 2021.01.
edge_cases: Calling an undefined function name: WARNING ('WARNING: Ignoring unknown function ...' - VERIFY text) and undef.
Calling a non-function value ((5)(1)): WARNING + undef (VERIFY text).
Named-argument shadowing a positional already bound: VERIFY behavior (warning + which wins).
Tail calls are eliminated since 2019.05 - millions of frames deep must work; non-tail recursion hits a bounded stack with a 'Recursion detected' style error (pin depth + message).
$-arguments propagate dynamically to everything the callee evaluates.
Functions/modules/variables are three namespaces: f=5; function f(x)=x; both coexist.
impl_notes: since=pre-2015.03 for named/positional binding; expression callees are 2021.01. Oracle-probe duplicate-binding and unknown-arg warning texts.

name: statement grammar (assignment, no expression statements)
signature: name = expr;  |  instantiation;  |  definitions  |  if/for/let statements  |  include/use
summary: Statements and expressions are disjoint grammars; assignment is last-write-wins per scope, not imperative.
semantics: Legal statements: 'name = expr;', module/function definitions, module instantiations (with optional modifier prefix and { } child block), module-level if/for/intersection_for/let, and include/use directives. There are no expression statements, no compound assignment (+=, ++), and geometry is not a value ('x = cube(1);' is an error). Within one scope, the LAST textual assignment to a name wins and takes effect at the position of the FIRST assignment, with 'WARNING: variable_name was reassigned' (VERIFY exact text).
edge_cases: a=1; b=a; a=2; yields b==2 - last-write-wins is observable and load-bearing (customizer -D overrides depend on it).
Assignments in { } blocks shadow; they never mutate outer scope.
No semicolon after a { } child block; ';' alone is an empty instantiation (VERIFY: bare ';' legality).
Modifier characters (* ! # %) may prefix exactly one instantiation.
'x = cube(1);' - VERIFY exact diagnostic (parse error vs 'unknown function cube' warning + undef, since cube is a module, not a function; believed the latter).
example: a=1; b=a; a=2; echo(b); // ECHO: 2 (with reassignment warning)
impl_notes: Implement scopes as ordered maps where reassignment replaces the expression at the original slot; pin interleaving with geometry statements via oracle.

name: abs
summary: Absolute value of a number.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

semantics: Returns |x| as a double (C fabs).
edge_cases: abs(nan) == nan; abs(-inf) == inf.
Non-numeric argument (vector, string, bool, undef): undef with WARNING (approx 'abs() parameter could not be converted' - VERIFY text).
No arguments / missing x: undef with WARNING (VERIFY).

name: sign
summary: Sign of a number as -1, 0, or 1.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

semantics: Returns -1 for x<0, 1 for x>0, 0 for x==0. Result is a plain number, never +-0.
edge_cases: sign(inf)==1, sign(-inf)==-1.
sign(nan): VERIFY - a comparison-based implementation returns 0; some return nan. Pin against oracle.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.

name: sin
summary: Sine of an angle given in DEGREES.

params.name: degrees
params.desc: Angle in degrees (any magnitude; reduced mod 360).

semantics: Returns sin of the angle interpreted in degrees. OpenSCAD special-cases angles that reduce to multiples of 90 degrees so results are EXACT: sin(180)==0 (not 1.2e-16), sin(90)==1, sin(30)==0.5 exactly — 30, 45 and 60 are special-cased in every quadrant alongside the 0/90/180/270 folding (degree-exact trig, 2019.05+).
edge_cases: DEGREES, not radians - the single most common porting error.

Exact values not just at quadrants but at 30/45/60 in EVERY quadrant: sin(30)==0.5, sin(45)==sqrt(1/2), sin(60)==sqrt(3)/2 exactly; angle folded/reduced first, so sin(36000)==0 exactly. Present in 2019.05 and 2021.01 (post-dates 2015.03).
sin(inf), sin(nan) -> nan (VERIFY warning; believed silent nan).
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Negative and >360 angles fine (periodic reduction).
|angle| >= 2^52 * 360 returns NaN for sin/cos/tan (deliberate total-precision-loss guard).
Inverse trig snaps to whole degrees when the whole-degree value round-trips: asin(1)==90 and acos(-1)==180 exactly.
impl_notes: Implement as sin(deg2rad(fmod-reduced angle)) with exact-value special cases for quadrant multiples; oracle-probe sin(45), sin(1e10).

name: cos
summary: Cosine of an angle in DEGREES with exact quadrant values.

params.name: degrees
params.desc: Angle in degrees.

semantics: cos in degrees; angles reducing to multiples of 90 return exact 0/1/-1: cos(90)==0 exactly, cos(180)==-1.
edge_cases: cos(90)==0 exactly (not 6.1e-17) - see sin for the exactness note; VERIFY introduction release.
cos(nan)/cos(inf) -> nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Hex-nut idiom depends on cos: r/cos(180/6); keep full double precision for non-special angles.
Same 30/45/60-in-every-quadrant exactness as sin: cos(60)==0.5 and cos(45)==sqrt(1/2) exactly (2019.05+).

name: tan
summary: Tangent of an angle in DEGREES.

params.name: degrees
params.desc: Angle in degrees.

semantics: tan in degrees; special-cased so tan(45)==1 and tan(180)==0 exactly.
edge_cases: tan(90) returns +inf and tan(270) returns -inf via explicit special case; tan(180) returns -0.0 internally — echo prints it as "0" (the 2021.01 formatter maps negative zero to "0"); the sign is observable only indirectly, e.g. 1/tan(180) == -inf.
tan(30)==1/sqrt(3), tan(45)==1, tan(60)==sqrt(3) exactly — 30/45/60 are special-cased in every quadrant (2019.05+).
tan(nan)/tan(inf) -> nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.

name: asin
summary: Arc sine returning DEGREES in [-90, 90].

params.name: x
params.desc: Number in [-1, 1].

semantics: Returns the angle in degrees whose sine is x. asin(1)==90, asin(0.5)==30, asin(-1)==-90.
edge_cases: |x|>1 -> nan, with WARNING in 2019.05+ (approx 'asin() out of range' - VERIFY text and presence).
asin(nan) -> nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Exactness: asin(1)==90 exactly, asin(0)==0 (VERIFY special-casing of results at quadrant values).

name: acos
summary: Arc cosine returning DEGREES in [0, 180].

params.name: x
params.desc: Number in [-1, 1].

semantics: Angle in degrees whose cosine is x. acos(1)==0, acos(0)==90, acos(-1)==180.
edge_cases: |x|>1 -> nan with WARNING (2019.05+; VERIFY text).
acos(nan) -> nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
acos(-1)==180 exactly (VERIFY).

name: atan
summary: Arc tangent returning DEGREES in (-90, 90).

params.name: x
params.desc: Any number.

semantics: Angle in degrees whose tangent is x. atan(1)==45.
edge_cases: atan(inf)==90, atan(-inf)==-90 (VERIFY exactness).
atan(nan) -> nan; non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Cannot distinguish quadrants - atan2 exists for that.

name: atan2
summary: Full-quadrant arc tangent of y/x, in DEGREES, range (-180, 180].

params.name: y
params.desc: Ordinate - FIRST argument.

params.name: x
params.desc: Abscissa - second argument.

semantics: Returns the angle of the point (x,y) in degrees using both signs to pick the quadrant: atan2(1,1)==45, atan2(1,-1)==135, atan2(-1,-1)==-135. Argument order is y then x (C convention).
edge_cases: atan2(0,0) == 0 (C behavior, no warning) - VERIFY.
Signed-zero corners follow C atan2: atan2(0,-1)==180, atan2(-0,-1)==-180 - VERIFY OpenSCAD preserves -0 distinctions.
atan2(y,x) with nan -> nan; non-numeric or missing arg: undef with WARNING.
Result exactly 90/180 at axis points (VERIFY exactness special-casing).
Degrees, unlike every other language's atan2.

name: floor
summary: Largest integral value <= x.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

semantics: C floor. floor(2.9)==2, floor(-2.1)==-3.
edge_cases: floor(-0)==-0 (VERIFY echo display).
floor(nan)==nan, floor(inf)==inf.
Values beyond 2^53 are already integral - returned unchanged.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.

name: ceil
summary: Smallest integral value >= x.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

edge_cases: ceil(-0.5)==-0 (negative zero result from C ceil - VERIFY echo display).
ceil(nan)==nan, ceil(inf)==inf.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Used by the $fa/$fs fragment formula - must match C ceil bit-for-bit or tessellation counts drift.

name: round
summary: Round to nearest integer, halves away from zero.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

semantics: Nearest integral value; ties round away from zero: round(2.5)==3, round(-2.5)==-3, round(2.4)==2.
edge_cases: VERIFY: half-away-from-zero via C round() - implementations differ (banker's rounding would give round(2.5)==2); pin round(0.5), round(-0.5), round(2.5), round(-2.5) against oracle.
round(-0.4)==-0 (VERIFY display).
round(nan)==nan, round(inf)==inf.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
No digits/precision parameter - users write round(x*100)/100.

name: ln
summary: NATURAL logarithm (base e).

params.name: x
params.desc: Number > 0.

semantics: C log(x). ln(exp(1))==1.
edge_cases: ln(0) -> -inf; VERIFY whether a warning is emitted (believed silent).
ln(negative) -> nan with WARNING in 2019.05+ (VERIFY text, approx 'ln() out of range').
ln(inf)==inf, ln(nan)==nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
Note the naming trap: ln is natural, log is base 10.

name: log
summary: BASE-10 logarithm (not natural).

params.name: x
params.desc: Number > 0.

edge_cases: Base 10, not e - the classic trap; there is no two-argument log(base,x) in 2021.01 (VERIFY - users write ln(x)/ln(b)).
log(0) -> -inf (VERIFY warning); log(negative) -> nan with WARNING (2019.05+).
log(nan)/non-numeric as ln.
log(100)==2 exactly (log10 exactness for powers of ten - VERIFY).

name: exp
summary: e raised to the power x.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number.

semantics: C exp(x). exp(1) is the idiom for the missing E constant.
edge_cases: Overflow (exp(1000)) -> inf, silently.
exp(-inf)==0, exp(nan)==nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
There is no E or TAU constant; only PI exists.

name: sqrt
summary: Square root.

params.name: x
params.desc: Number >= 0.

semantics: C sqrt(x).
edge_cases: sqrt(negative) -> nan with WARNING (2019.05+; VERIFY text, approx 'sqrt() out of range' or 'sqrt of negative').
sqrt(-0)==-0 (IEEE; VERIFY display).
sqrt(inf)==inf, sqrt(nan)==nan.
Non-numeric: undef with WARNING.
No cbrt builtin; users write pow(x,1/3) which is nan for negative x.

name: pow
summary: base raised to exponent; the pre-2021.01 spelling of ^.

params.name: base
params.desc: Number.

params.name: exponent
params.desc: Number.

semantics: C pow(base, exponent). Identical math to the ^ operator (2021.01).
edge_cases: pow(0,0)==1; pow(0,-1)==inf; pow(-8, 1/3)==nan (negative base, non-integer exponent).
Missing exponent (pow(2)): undef with WARNING (VERIFY).
Non-numeric args: undef with WARNING.
Not deprecated in 2021.01 - both spellings must work forever; keep them byte-identical in behavior.
pow(nan,0)==1 per C - VERIFY OpenSCAD matches.

name: min
summary: Minimum of two-or-more arguments, or of a single vector's elements.

params.name: a, b, ...
params.desc: Two or more numbers (VERIFY: strings also comparable - see edge cases).

params.name: vector
params.desc: Alternative single argument: a vector whose elements are compared.

semantics: With >=2 arguments, returns the smallest; with exactly one vector argument, returns the smallest element. Comparison is the relational < ordering.
edge_cases: min([]) (empty vector): WARNING + undef (approx 'min() parameter could not be converted' or 'empty vector' - VERIFY text).
min(5) with a single scalar: VERIFY - believed WARNING + undef (one argument must be a vector).
Strings: VERIFY whether min("a","b") works lexicographically or is undef - pin against oracle.
Mixed/mismatched element types in the vector: undef with WARNING (VERIFY).
nan among arguments: result order-dependent under C comparisons - pin min(nan,1) and min(1,nan) against oracle (VERIFY).
Nested vectors as elements: VERIFY (believed undef - no deep min).
min(vector, scalar) two-arg mix: undef with WARNING (VERIFY).

The single-vector form (min([a,b,c])) was added in 2015.03; earlier releases warn/return undef for a vector argument. It compares with the generic relational less-than, so a vector of strings returns the lexicographic extreme (see string comparison).
impl_notes: The 1-vector vs n-scalar dispatch and every degenerate case need oracle pinning; libraries call both forms.

name: max
summary: Maximum of two-or-more arguments, or of a single vector's elements.

params.name: a, b, ...
params.desc: Two or more numbers.

params.name: vector
params.desc: Alternative single vector argument.

semantics: Mirror of min with > ordering; identical dispatch rules.
edge_cases: max([]) -> WARNING + undef.
max(5) single scalar: VERIFY (believed WARNING + undef).
nan handling, string handling, mixed types: same VERIFY set as min - keep the two functions exactly symmetric.
Used pervasively in fragment sizing (cylinder uses max(r1,r2)) - numeric behavior must be exact.

The single-vector form (max([a,b,c])) was added in 2015.03; earlier releases warn/return undef for a vector argument. It compares with the generic relational less-than, so a vector of strings returns the lexicographic extreme (see string comparison).

name: norm
summary: Euclidean length of a numeric vector of any dimension.

params.name: v
params.desc: Vector of numbers (any length).

semantics: Returns sqrt(sum of squares of elements). Works for any dimension: norm([3,4])==5, norm([1,1,1,1])==2.
edge_cases: norm([]) == 0 (empty sum) - VERIFY.
Any non-numeric element (string, vector, undef, bool): undef with WARNING (VERIFY: whether nested numeric vectors are rejected - believed yes, no Frobenius norm).
norm of a string: VERIFY - believed undef (some docs mention strings; pin it).
norm(scalar) / norm(undef): undef with WARNING.
Elements of inf -> inf; nan element -> nan.
Overflow: naive sum-of-squares overflows around 1e154 -> inf; VERIFY OpenSCAD is naive (no hypot-style scaling) and clone that.

name: cross
summary: Vector cross product: 3-vectors give a 3-vector; 2-vectors give the scalar z-component (2019.05+).

params.name: a
params.desc: Numeric vector of length 3 (or 2, since 2015.03).

params.name: b
params.desc: Numeric vector of the SAME length as a.

semantics: For 3-vectors returns [a1*b2-a2*b1, a2*b0-a0*b2, a0*b1-a1*b0]. For two 2-vectors returns the scalar a0*b1-a1*b0. Both arguments must have the same length, 2 or 3.
edge_cases: Length mismatch (3 with 2) or lengths other than 2/3: undef with WARNING (approx 'Invalid parameters for cross()' - VERIFY text).
2D form since 2015.03 (returns the scalar v0[0]*v1[1] - v0[1]*v1[0]); only 2014.03-era releases warned/returned undef for 2-vectors.
Non-numeric elements: undef with WARNING (VERIFY vs nan propagation).
Missing second argument: undef with WARNING.
No n-ary or chained form; exactly two arguments.
impl_notes: since marks the material 2D change; 3D form is pre-2015.03.

name: PI
summary: Built-in constant 3.14159265358979... (full double precision M_PI).
semantics: A predefined variable in the outermost scope holding pi as a double. Not a keyword - it is an ordinary (non-$) variable name.
edge_cases: echo(PI) prints 3.14159 (6-significant-digit %g formatting), but the stored value is full precision.
There is NO E constant (users write exp(1)) and no TAU.

User code CAN assign PI = 3; shadowing/overriding it - VERIFY whether a reassignment warning fires and whether builtins (nothing consumes PI internally - they use their own constant) are affected (they are not).
Case-sensitive: pi is an unknown variable (undef + warning).

name: is_undef
summary: True iff x is undef; uniquely suppresses the unknown-variable warning, acting as a defined() guard.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any expression; a bare never-defined variable name is probed silently.

semantics: Returns true when the argument evaluates to undef, false otherwise. SPECIAL: is_undef(foo) where foo was never assigned returns true WITHOUT the usual 'unknown variable' WARNING that a bare reference would emit - the documented way to test for optional/overridable variables.
edge_cases: The warning suppression scope: VERIFY whether it covers only a bare variable argument or any expression (is_undef(foo+1) - believed the lookup inside still warns; pin it).
is_undef(undef)==true; is_undef(0)==false, is_undef(nan)==false, is_undef([])==false, is_undef(false)==false.
A missing function parameter (no default, not passed) is undef -> true.
v[99] out-of-range feeds is_undef true - the idiom for end-of-list in recursion.
No arguments: VERIFY (error vs true).
Introduced 2019.05; before that, scripts compared x==undef (which also works, since == is total).
impl_notes: Implement the silent-lookup special case in the evaluator, not the function - it changes warning emission, which --hardwarnings turns fatal.

name: is_num
summary: True for finite and infinite numbers; FALSE for nan.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Returns true iff x is of number type AND is not nan. This nan exclusion is documented upstream behavior: is_num(0/0) is false.
edge_cases: is_num(0/0)==false - the nan carve-out is the trap; nan IS stored as a number but tests false.
is_num(1/0)==true - inf is believed to test TRUE (VERIFY against oracle, per seed).
is_num(-0)==true.
is_num(true)==false (no coercion), is_num("1")==false, is_num(undef)==false, is_num([1])==false, is_num(range)==false.
No args: VERIFY.
example: echo(is_num(3), is_num(0/0), is_num(1/0)); // ECHO: true, false, true
impl_notes: Implement as type==number && !isnan(value); pin the inf case.

name: is_bool
summary: True iff x is exactly true or false.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Type test for the boolean type. No truthiness involved: only the two boolean values pass.
edge_cases: is_bool(0)==false, is_bool(1)==false, is_bool("true")==false, is_bool(undef)==false.
Result of comparisons and !/&&/|| is boolean, so is_bool(1==1)==true.
No args: VERIFY.

name: is_string
summary: True iff x is a string.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Type test for strings, including "".
edge_cases: is_string("")==true.
is_string(str(5))==true - str always yields a string.
A 1-character indexing result s[0] is a string -> true; there is no char type.
is_string(["a"])==false; is_string(undef)==false.
No args: VERIFY.

name: is_list
summary: True iff x is a vector (including []); FALSE for strings and ranges.

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Type test for the vector/list type. Nested and heterogeneous vectors pass; the empty vector passes.
edge_cases: is_list([])==true.
is_list("abc")==false - strings iterate like lists in comprehensions but are NOT lists.
is_list([0:5])==false - ranges are a distinct type; since there is no is_range, a range is only detectable by elimination (!is_list && !is_num && !is_string && !is_bool && !is_undef && !is_function).
is_list(undef)==false.
No args: VERIFY.
example: echo(is_list([]), is_list("ab"), is_list([0:2])); // ECHO: true, false, false
impl_notes: The elimination-based range detection idiom appears in libraries - all six sibling tests must be consistent.

name: is_object
summary: SNAPSHOT-ONLY: type test for the experimental object (dict-like) type returned by textmetrics()/fontmetrics().

params.name: x
params.desc: Any value.

semantics: Returns true iff x is an object value - a key/value structure with dot access, produced only by snapshot-gated features (--enable=textmetrics and later object literals in newer nightlies). Not present in 2021.01.
edge_cases: In 2021.01 calling is_object is an unknown-function WARNING + undef - a 2021.01-compat implementation should reproduce that unless snapshot features are opted in.
is_object([])==false, is_object(undef)==false - objects are distinct from vectors.
The object type itself is a moving snapshot target (object literals, has_key etc. in 2024+ nightlies) - VERIFY per-snapshot if chasing snapshot parity.
Decide-and-document: implement behind an --enable flag mirroring upstream, or omit with the faithful unknown-function warning.
example:
// snapshot only, --enable=textmetrics
tm = textmetrics("hi"); echo(is_object(tm)); // ECHO: true

name: str
signature: str(value, ...) -> string  (zero or more arguments of any type)
summary: Converts every argument to its display text and concatenates them into one string; the ONLY string concatenation mechanism in the language.

params.name: value, ...
params.desc: Any number of values of any type (number, string, boolean, vector, range, undef, function literal). Each is converted to its textual form and appended in order. Zero arguments allowed.

semantics: Each argument is rendered using the exact same value formatter that echo uses, with one asymmetry: a string passed DIRECTLY as an argument is inserted unquoted, whereas echo would quote it. Strings nested inside vector arguments ARE quoted, exactly as in echo. Numbers are formatted by the shared 6-significant-digit double-conversion formatter: integers print without a decimal point, trailing zeros are trimmed, fixed notation covers 1e-5 <= |x| < 1e6, and scientific notation with an unpadded exponent is used outside that range. Booleans render as true/false, undef as undef, vectors as [a, b, c] (comma+space, recursive), ranges in spaced-colon form, function literals as a source-like rendering. The results are concatenated with no separators. str never fails and never warns; every value has a rendering.
edge_cases: str() with zero arguments returns "" (empty string).
Number formatting is 6 significant digits: str(1/3) == "0.333333", str(PI) == "3.14159", str(10.0) == "10" (no decimal point for integral values), trailing zeros trimmed.

Scientific switch at 1e6: str(1000000) == "1e+6", str(1234567) == "1.23457e+6" — large integers go scientific AND GET ROUNDED (famous trap; user code that builds numbers into strings inherits this loss).
Small magnitudes: str(0.0001) == "0.0001" AND str(0.00001) == "0.00001" — fixed notation persists down to 1e-5; scientific only below it, unpadded: str(1.1e-6) == "1.1e-6", str(1e100) == "1e+100".
str(1/0) == "inf" (after the division-by-zero WARNING from the division itself), str(-1/0) == "-inf", str(0/0) == "nan".
Negative zero renders as "0" (UNIQUE_ZERO in the 2021.01 formatter); its sign is observable only via arithmetic (1/-0 == -inf).
Top-level string args are unquoted: str("a","b") == "ab" — this is THE concatenation idiom; echo(str(...)) vs echo(...) differ in string quoting.
Strings nested inside vector arguments are quoted: str(["a"]) == "[\"a\"]". VERIFY: interior quotes/backslashes in such nested strings are NOT re-escaped in the output (echo("a\"b") style probes).
Booleans -> "true"/"false"; undef -> "undef"; empty vector -> "[]"; nested vectors recursive with ", " separators.
VERIFY: ranges render with spaces and explicit step even when implicit: str([0:10]) believed "[0 : 1 : 10]" (pin whether implicit step 1 is displayed).
VERIFY: function-literal arguments render as source-like text, e.g. "function(x, y = 1) x + y" (pin exact spacing/body serialization).
str never emits warnings or errors regardless of argument types — total function.
Formatting is identical between str, echo, and the assert-message renderer; a single shared formatter is compatibility-critical because golden .echo output and user string-building both depend on it.
VERIFY: dev snapshots have moved toward full-precision shortest-roundtrip number output — 2021.01 baseline must keep 6-significant-digit double-conversion output.
impl_notes: Implement ONE shared value-to-text formatter used by str/echo/assert. Pin via oracle probes: magnitude sweep 10^-7..10^9, negative values, -0, 0.1+0.2, inf/nan, nested vectors with strings containing quotes/backslashes, ranges with and without explicit step, function literals. Deep recursive str() accumulation must not be O(n^2) — use ropes or amortized buffers; libraries build long strings recursively.

name: chr
signature: chr(n, ...) -> string  where each argument is a number, a vector of numbers, or a range
summary: Converts Unicode code point number(s) to a string; multiple arguments, vector arguments and range arguments all concatenate.

params.name: n, ...
params.desc: Each argument: a code point number, a vector of code point numbers, or a range of code points. All resulting characters are concatenated in argument order.

semantics: Each numeric value is interpreted as a Unicode code point and converted to the corresponding character; all characters from all arguments are concatenated into one string encoded as UTF-8. Vector arguments contribute one character per element; range arguments are expanded and contribute one character per step. Invalid code points contribute nothing (empty string) rather than erroring.
edge_cases: chr(65) == "A"; multiple scalar args concatenate: chr(65, 97) == "Aa" (documented form).
Vector argument: chr([104, 105]) == "hi"; range argument: chr([65:70]) == "ABCDEF" (range expanded, inclusive endpoints per normal range semantics).
Code point 0 contributes an empty string; negative values contribute empty. VERIFY: values > 0x10FFFF contribute empty (pin exact upper-bound behavior).
VERIFY: surrogate code points U+D800..U+DFFF — believed to produce nothing/invalid output; pin against oracle since a strict UTF-8 encoder must decide.
VERIFY: non-integer values truncate toward zero (chr(65.7) believed "A"); pin truncation vs rounding.
Non-numeric arguments (string, boolean, undef) contribute nothing. VERIFY: whether a WARNING like "chr() parameter could not be converted" is emitted or it is silent.
chr() with no arguments returns "". VERIFY zero-arg acceptance without warning.
Astral-plane code points work and produce a single character counted once by len: len(chr(128169)) == 1.
VERIFY: nested vectors inside a vector argument (chr([[65]])) — believed to contribute nothing; pin.
Roundtrip law for valid inputs: ord(chr(n)) == n; chr(ord(s)) == first character of s.
Introduced in 2015.03; in older interpreters an unknown-function WARNING plus undef.
impl_notes: Requires a real code-point-to-UTF-8 encoder. Oracle probes: chr(0), chr(-1), chr(55296) (surrogate), chr(1114111), chr(1114112), chr(65.5), chr("x"), chr(). Match silent-vs-warning behavior exactly because --hardwarnings turns any warning into a fatal error.

name: ord
summary: Returns the Unicode code point of the FIRST character of a string.

params.name: s
params.desc: A string. Only the first character (first code point) is examined; the rest is ignored.

semantics: Decodes the first Unicode code point of the UTF-8 string and returns it as a number. Inverse of chr for single characters. Typically combined with comprehensions to convert whole strings: [for (c = s) ord(c)].
edge_cases: ord("a") == 97; ord("abc") == 97 (first code point only, silently ignores the rest).
ord("") -> undef.

Non-string argument (number, vector, boolean, undef) -> undef. VERIFY: whether the WARNING "ord() parameter could not be converted" (2019.05-era conversion-warning family) is emitted or the failure is silent.
Operates on code points, not grapheme clusters: for a decomposed "é" style string, ord returns 101 (the 'e'), and the combining mark is a separate character reachable via s[1].
Astral characters return the full code point (> 0xFFFF), counted as one character: ord of an emoji like U+1F60A returns 128522 — requires true UTF-8 decoding, not UTF-16 surrogate halves.
Result is an ordinary double; safe in arithmetic and chr roundtrips.
2019.05+ only: on 2015.03 the call produces an unknown-function WARNING and undef — libraries feature-test with version_num() >= 20190500.
impl_notes: Trivial once strings are stored/decoded as UTF-8 with code-point iteration. Pin the non-string and empty-string warning behavior via oracle. Ensure no surrogate-pair splitting for astral input.

name: string indexing s[i]
summary: Zero-based code-point indexing into a string; yields a one-character STRING (there is no char type); anything out of range yields undef.

params.name: s
params.desc: The string being indexed.

params.name: i
params.desc: Zero-based code-point index; must be a non-negative integer number within [0, len(s)).

semantics: s[i] returns the i-th Unicode code point of s as a new string of length 1. Indexing is by code point over the UTF-8 storage, never by byte. Any index that is negative, >= len(s), non-integer, or non-numeric yields undef. There is no slicing and no negative-from-end indexing; substring extraction is user-space via comprehensions plus str, or recursion.
edge_cases: Result is a string: "abc"[0] == "a", and ("abc"[0])[0] == "a" — chained indexing of the 1-char result works.
Out of range (i >= len(s)) -> undef. Negative i -> undef (no Python-style wrapping). VERIFY: both are silent, with no console warning.
VERIFY: non-integer index (s[1.5]) -> undef, with no rounding; pin whether exactly-integral doubles like 2.0 index normally (they do).
Index of boolean/string/undef/vector type -> undef. VERIFY: indexing a string with a range or vector yields undef (no fancy multi-index).
Code-point correctness: "häx"[1] == "ä"; an astral emoji occupies exactly one index position. Byte-based indexing corrupts any non-ASCII text and is a compatibility bug.
Indexing the empty string always yields undef.
Grapheme clusters are NOT units: a decomposed accent occupies two indices (base + combining mark).
The same postfix [] operator serves vectors; dispatch is by operand type at runtime.
undef[0] -> undef. VERIFY: silent vs warning.
impl_notes: Store strings as UTF-8 but index by code point; for performance either cache a code-point offset table per string or accept O(i) scans (real scripts index in loops — memoize). Oracle probes: negative, fractional, huge, and non-numeric indices; multibyte and astral content.

name: string iteration
summary: Strings are iterable per character (per code point), each iteration binding a 1-character string.
semantics: In list comprehensions, a string used as the iterable produces one iteration per Unicode code point, binding a one-character string each time: [for (c = "abc") c] == ["a", "b", "c"]. This is the primitive from which user-space split/map/upper/lower are built. Combined with search(), ord(), chr() and str() it forms the whole string-processing toolkit — there are no substring/split/join/replace/case builtins anywhere in the language.
edge_cases: [for (c = "abc") c] -> ["a", "b", "c"]; empty string -> zero iterations -> [].
Iteration is per code point: multibyte and astral characters are single iterations; combining marks iterate separately from their base.

VERIFY: the statement-level for MODULE also iterates strings character-wise in 2021.01 (for (c = "ab") translate(...) ...) — pin the exact version coverage; older releases may have treated the string as a single scalar iteration.

VERIFY: 'each' applied to a string splices characters ([each "ab"] believed ["a", "b"]) — pin, since each on a non-list normally yields the value itself and strings sit ambiguously between 'iterable' and 'scalar'.
Characters come back as strings, so nested iteration over an iterated character iterates that 1-char string once.

Reversal/mapping idioms rely on this: str-join of a comprehension is the canonical map: str([for(c=s) ...]) does NOT join (it renders a vector) — joining requires recursion or a fold via str(acc, c). Reimplementation must keep these idioms fast.
search() with a string match_value iterates its characters as independent search terms — same per-character model (see search entry).
impl_notes: Iterator over UTF-8 code points shared by comprehensions, the for module, each, and search's per-character term expansion. Pin the for-module and each cases against the oracle before freezing (two VERIFY items above).

name: string comparison
summary: Equality is total deep equality; relational operators are defined for string-string only and compare lexicographically by Unicode code point.
semantics: == and != work across all types: two strings are equal iff they have identical code-point sequences; a string compared to any non-string is unequal (false, not undef). The relational operators < <= > >= are defined only between two strings (or two numbers): they compare lexicographically by code point, case-sensitively, with no locale, collation, or normalization. A relational comparison where either side is not the right type yields undef.
edge_cases: "a" == "a" -> true; "a" == 97 -> false (mismatched types compare unequal under ==, never undef).
"abc" < "abd" -> true; "ab" < "abc" -> true (proper prefix sorts first); "" < "a" -> true.
Case-sensitive code-point order: "Z" < "a" is true (90 < 97); digits sort before uppercase before lowercase.
"a" < 5 -> undef (relational across types is undef, not false). VERIFY: whether a WARNING like "undefined operation (string < number)" accompanies it in 2021.01.
No Unicode normalization: NFC and NFD spellings of the same visual text are DIFFERENT, unequal strings.
Implementation shortcut that is exactly conformant: byte-wise comparison of UTF-8 encodings yields the same order as code-point comparison (UTF-8 is order-preserving) — safe to use.
Sorting user-space (there is no builtin sort) is built on these operators; nan-style partiality does not apply to strings, but comparing a string against undef relationally is undef.

min/max: the n-ary form min(a,b,...) is numbers-only (a non-number argument yields the conversion WARNING + undef), but the single-vector form uses the generic relational less-than, so min(["b","a"]) returns "a" (lexicographic) in 2021.01; mixed-type element vectors give unwarned, comparator-dependent results.
impl_notes: Use memcmp-style byte comparison over UTF-8. Pin the warning-vs-silent behavior of mixed-type relational comparisons via oracle (matters under --hardwarnings).

name: no string + concatenation
summary: There is NO + concatenation for strings — arithmetic operators on strings yield undef with a console warning; str() is the only concatenation mechanism.
semantics: All arithmetic operators (+ - * / % and unary minus) are undefined for string operands. Applying them yields undef and emits a console WARNING, and evaluation continues (undef then propagates through the expression). Concatenation is exclusively via str(a, b, ...); character-level assembly can also go through chr(concat(...)) over code points.
edge_cases: "a" + "b" -> undef with WARNING. Approximate 2021.01 text: 'WARNING: undefined operation ("a" + "b") in file <path>, line <N>' — VERIFY exact operand rendering (values vs type names) against the oracle; users and CI parse this text.
Same undef+WARNING for "a" - "b", "a" * 2, "a" / 2, "a" % 2, and unary -"a".
string + number, number + string: undef + WARNING (no coercion in either direction).
The undef result is falsy and poisons downstream arithmetic silently after the single warning at the failing operation.
Under --hardwarnings the warning is FATAL — a reimplementation that 'helpfully' implements + concatenation both diverges observably and hides bugs scripts rely on catching.
str("a", "b") == "ab" is the canonical replacement; repeated in loops it is the standard (O(n^2) if naive) string-building pattern.
== on strings still works normally; only arithmetic is undefined.
impl_notes: Emit exactly one warning per failing operation evaluation (per loop iteration if in a loop). Pin the warning wording verbatim via oracle; it is part of the observable surface.

name: string Unicode model
signature: "..." literals; UTF-8 storage; code-point semantics for len/[]/ord/iteration
summary: Strings are immutable UTF-8 sequences whose observable unit everywhere (len, indexing, ord, iteration, search) is the Unicode code point.
semantics: String literals are double-quoted, may contain arbitrary UTF-8 directly in the source file, and support the escapes \" \\ \t \n \r plus \x##, \u#### and \U###### (since 2015.03). At runtime a string is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points: len counts code points, s[i] indexes code points, ord/chr convert code points, iteration and search operate per code point. There is no char type (1-char strings serve), no mutation, no byte-level access.
edge_cases: len("häx") == 3 despite 4 UTF-8 bytes; one astral emoji has len 1 despite 4 bytes.
\u####/\U######/\x## escapes exist since 2015.03 (raw UTF-8 in source also works). VERIFY: what an unknown escape like \q produces (believed the character literally) — must match.
Escapes \t \n \r produce real control characters that echo prints literally inside the quoted rendering (a \n in a string breaks the ECHO line). VERIFY exact console rendering of embedded newlines.
No normalization is ever applied — comparison, len and indexing see exactly the code points written.
Grapheme clusters are not a unit anywhere in the language.
VERIFY: behavior on invalid UTF-8 (possible via file reading or malformed source): believed replacement/undefined — pin if import paths can produce it.
text() consumes these strings for glyph shaping; corrupting non-ASCII via byte indexing shows up visibly there.
Strings are valid dictionary-order keys nowhere (no maps in 2021.01); vectors of [key,value] pairs plus search() serve that role.
impl_notes: Represent as UTF-8 with code-point-aware ops. The escape-set and unknown-escape behavior belongs to the lexer team but the runtime contract here is: code points everywhere, bytes nowhere.

name: concat
signature: concat(a, b, ...) -> vector  (zero or more arguments)
summary: Single-level list concatenation: list arguments contribute their elements, non-list arguments (INCLUDING strings) are appended as single elements; never deep-flattens.

params.name: a, b, ...
params.desc: Any values. A vector argument contributes its top-level elements in order; any non-vector argument (number, string, boolean, range, undef, function) is appended as one element.

semantics: Builds a new vector by walking the arguments left to right: for each vector argument, append its elements (one level only — nested vectors stay nested); for each non-vector argument, append the value itself. The result is always a fresh vector; inputs are never modified (nothing in the language mutates).
edge_cases: concat([1], [2,3]) == [1, 2, 3]; single-level only: concat([[1]], [2]) == [[1], 2] — inner vectors are NOT flattened.
Non-list args append whole: concat(1, 2) == [1, 2]; concat([1,2], 3) == [1, 2, 3].
STRINGS ARE NOT LISTS here: concat("ab", "cd") == ["ab", "cd"] — no character splicing and no string concatenation (a classic wrong expectation; str() concatenates strings).
concat() with zero arguments returns []. VERIFY: accepted silently with no warning.
undef arguments are kept: concat(undef) == [undef]; concat([], undef, []) == [undef].
VERIFY: a range argument is appended as a single range VALUE, not expanded: concat([1], [2:4]) believed [1, [2 : 1 : 4]] (echo rendering); expansion requires each/comprehension.
Booleans and function literals append as single elements.
Empty-vector args contribute nothing: concat([], []) == [].
2015.03+: earlier interpreters emit unknown-function WARNING and undef; libraries polyfilled concat with comprehensions.
Amortized-O(1) append matters: comprehension+concat chains in recursive library code (pre-'each' style: concat(acc, [x])) are hot paths.
impl_notes: Straightforward; the two behaviors to pin via oracle are zero-arg concat() and range-argument handling. Keep persistent/rope-style vectors or copy-on-append with amortization — recursive concat accumulation is ubiquitous in pre-BOSL2 libraries.

name: len
summary: Element count of a vector or code-point count of a string; undef for every other type (numbers, booleans, ranges, undef, functions).

params.name: value
params.desc: A vector (returns top-level element count) or a string (returns number of Unicode code points). Any other type yields undef.

semantics: For vectors, returns the number of top-level elements (nested vectors count as one element each). For strings, returns the number of Unicode code points (not bytes; astral characters count 1). For any other type — number, boolean, undef, range, function literal — the result is undef. Ranges deliberately have no len: they are a distinct non-list type.
edge_cases: len("häx") == 3 (code points, not bytes); len("") == 0; a single astral emoji has len 1.

len(5), len(true), len(undef), len(function(x) x) -> undef. VERIFY: whether 2021.01 emits a WARNING of the "len() parameter could not be converted" conversion-failure family or returns undef silently — pin exact text; --hardwarnings users depend on the set of warnings.

len([0:10]) -> undef — ranges are not lists (is_list false); the only way to size a range is to expand it or compute from begin/step/end (which are themselves not extractable in 2021.01 — no accessors).
len is the standard guard in recursive list processing (i >= len(v) base case); it must be O(1).
len of the result of search/concat/comprehensions behaves as for any vector.
No arguments or multiple arguments: VERIFY error/warning behavior (believed too-many/too-few argument warning with undef).
impl_notes: O(1) for vectors; for strings either store code-point count eagerly or cache on first query. Oracle probes: len on every type including ranges and function values, plus the warning text question.

name: search
signature: search(match_value, string_or_vector, num_returns_per_match = 1, index_col_num = 0) -> vector (shape depends on num_returns_per_match)
summary: Per-term index lookup in a string, flat vector, or table — with per-CHARACTER expansion of string search terms and mode-dependent ragged result shapes that must be cloned bug-for-bug.

params.name: match_value
params.desc: The search term(s). A STRING is split into one term PER CHARACTER (it is NOT substring search). A vector supplies one term per element (elements may be strings, numbers, or other values). A bare scalar acts as a single term (VERIFY acceptance).

params.name: string_or_vector
params.desc: The target: a string (terms compared against each character), a flat vector (terms compared against each element), or a table — a vector of row-vectors — where terms are compared against row[index_col_num].

params.name: num_returns_per_match
params.desc: Default 1: return only the FIRST match index per term, as a BARE index in a flat result. 0: return ALL match indices per term, as one sub-vector per term. N>1: up to N match indices per term, as one sub-vector per term.

params.name: index_col_num
params.desc: Default 0. When target rows are vectors, the column within each row that terms are compared against. Ignored for string targets and plain scalar elements (VERIFY).

semantics: search runs an independent scan of the target for each search term and combines per-term results into one output vector, in term order. Matching uses the language's == equality (so type-mismatched comparisons simply never match). Result shape is mode-dependent and deliberately irregular: with num_returns_per_match=1 the output is a FLAT vector of bare indices; with 0 or N>1 the output is a vector of sub-vectors, one per term, each holding that term's match indices in ascending target order (empty sub-vector [] for a term with no match). Because a string match_value explodes into per-character terms, search("abc", s) finds the characters a, b, c separately — to search for a whole string as an element of a list you must wrap it: search(["abc"], list).
edge_cases: Per-character terms: search("a","abcdabcd") == [0]; search("ab","abcdabcd") == [0,1]; search("ba","abcdabcd") == [1,0] (result order follows TERM order, not target order); search("aa","aa") == [0,0] (duplicate terms searched independently).
All-matches mode: search("a","abcdabcd",0) == [[0,4]]; search("ab","abcdabcd",0) == [[0,4],[1,5]].

No-match, default mode: search("e","abcdabcd") == [] — the documented example. VERIFY (critical, two candidate behaviors): with num_returns_per_match=1, an unmatched term is believed to be SKIPPED ENTIRELY from the flat output (so the result can be SHORTER than the term list and indices cannot be aligned back to terms — the documented reason to use mode 0), accompanied by a console message approximately 'WARNING: search term not found: "e"'; the alternative candidate is that the term contributes an [] element producing mixed shapes like [0, [], 2]. Pin against the oracle and clone exactly — libraries pattern-match this.
No-match in modes 0 / N>1: the term's slot holds [] — search("abe","abcd",0) == [[0],[1],[]] — ragged shapes are normal and load-bearing.
VERIFY: the not-found console message — exact wording, whether it appears in all modes or only default mode, and once per missing term.

Whole-string element search requires wrapping: search(["b"], ["a","b","c"]) == [1]; bare search("b", ["a","b","c"]) also finds index 1 but ONLY because the term is a single character comparing equal to the 1-char string elements; a multi-character term (from a wrapped list) compares whole-element.

Table search: search("b", [["a",1],["b",2],["b",3]], 0) == [[1,2]] (comparing column 0); with index_col_num=1: search(2, [["a",1],["b",2]], 0, 1) == [[1]] (VERIFY scalar match_value acceptance here; wrap as [2] if the oracle warns).
VERIFY: scalar (number/boolean) match_value as a single term on a flat vector: search(3, [5,3,3]) believed [1]; pin whether a warning demands a list.
num_returns_per_match=N>1 returns AT MOST N indices, fewer if fewer matches exist: search("a","aaaa",3) == [[0,1,2]]... VERIFY exact — believed [[0,1,2]].
VERIFY: negative or fractional num_returns_per_match — believed truncated to int; pin whether negative behaves like 0 (all) or errors.
Empty match_value ("" or []) -> []; empty target -> every term unmatched (mode-dependent shape).
Type-strict matching: number 1 never matches string "1"; undef terms — VERIFY whether undef==undef equality lets an undef term match undef elements.

VERIFY: rows shorter than index_col_num, or scalar rows in a table search — believed console warning (approx 'search: invalid table') with the row skipped; pin text and whether the term can still match later valid rows.
VERIFY: vector-valued terms matching vector elements/columns via deep equality — believed to work (== is deep); pin.
VERIFY: index_col_num with a string target — believed ignored/invalid; pin.
Matching is always by equality — no wildcards, no regex, no substring, no case folding, anywhere.
impl_notes: This is the most quirk-dense builtin; write an exhaustive oracle probe matrix over {string/list/scalar match_value} x {string/flat/table target} x {num_returns 1,0,2} x {hit, miss, multi-hit} x {invalid rows} and freeze every output shape and console message verbatim BEFORE implementing. Do not normalize the ragged shapes or 'fix' the mode-1 miss behavior — BOSL2-era and Thingiverse code depends on the exact quirks.

name: lookup
signature: lookup(key, table) -> number  where table = [[k0,v0],[k1,v1],...] with numeric keys in ascending order
summary: Piecewise-LINEAR interpolation of values over a numeric key table, clamped to the first/last value outside the key range.

params.name: key
params.desc: Numeric lookup key.

params.name: table
params.desc: Vector of [key, value] pairs; keys and values numeric; keys expected in ascending order.

semantics: If key exactly equals a table key, the stored value is returned exactly. If key falls between two neighboring keys k_i < key < k_j, the result is linear interpolation v_i + (v_j - v_i) * (key - k_i) / (k_j - k_i). If key is below the smallest key, the FIRST value is returned; above the largest key, the LAST value — i.e. the function clamps, it never extrapolates. Canonical uses: gear/thread tables, animation easing over $t.
edge_cases: Exact hit returns the stored value with no interpolation arithmetic (bit-exact): lookup(0.5, [[0,0],[0.5,1],[1,0]]) == 1.
Clamping: lookup(-99, t) == first value; lookup(99, t) == last value; key = +/-inf clamps likewise (VERIFY inf handling).
Single-pair table -> that value for every key.
Empty table -> undef. VERIFY: accompanying WARNING text (a lookup-specific message exists in the conversion-warning family; pin wording).
VERIFY: duplicate/equal adjacent keys — interpolating between them divides by zero; pin whether the result is the stored value (exact-hit path wins), nan, or inf.

VERIFY: unsorted tables — the documented contract requires ascending keys; the actual algorithm (believed nearest-bracketing scan) may still produce SOME deterministic answer on unsorted input; pin the exact behavior rather than asserting, because sloppy real-world tables exist.
VERIFY: rows with extra columns ([k, v, junk]) — believed extra entries ignored; rows that are scalars or wrong-typed — believed warning + row skipped or undef result; pin.
Non-numeric key (string/undef/vector) -> undef (VERIFY warning); key = nan -> VERIFY (comparisons with nan all fail; candidate outcomes: first value, last value, or nan — pin exactly).
Values must be scalars in 2021.01 — no vector-valued interpolation (feature exists only as later discussion/snapshot work); vector values -> VERIFY undef/warning.
Table itself non-vector -> undef + VERIFY warning.
impl_notes: Pin the degenerate-table behaviors (empty, duplicate keys, unsorted, nan key) via oracle probes before choosing an implementation — a binary search implementation and a linear bracketing scan agree on well-formed input but can diverge on unsorted tables, and real scripts feed it garbage.

name: vector addition and subtraction
signature: v1 + v2, v1 - v2, -v  (equal-length vectors, recursive elementwise); vector/scalar mixes -> undef
summary: Elementwise + and - on EQUAL-length vectors (recursing into nested vectors); NO scalar broadcasting — scalar+vector and length mismatches yield undef with a warning.
semantics: When both operands are vectors of the same length, + and - operate elementwise, recursing into nested vectors (so matrices add naturally). Unary minus negates elementwise recursively. There is NO broadcasting: a scalar added to a vector, or two vectors of different lengths, produce undef and a console WARNING, and evaluation continues. Elementwise recursion applies the same rules at each level, so mismatches deep inside a structure surface as undef at that position or for that sub-operation.
edge_cases: Length mismatch: [1,2] + [1,2,3] -> undef with WARNING (approx 'undefined operation ([1, 2] + [1, 2, 3])' — VERIFY exact operand rendering). VERIFY: ancient pre-2015 releases truncated to the shorter length; 2021.01 must be undef+warn.
NO broadcasting: [1,2] + 1 -> undef + WARNING; 1 + [1,2] likewise; users write [for (x=v) x+1].

VERIFY: element-level type mismatch inside equal-length vectors ([1,"a"] + [1,2]) — believed to produce undef AT THAT ELEMENT ([2, undef]) with a warning, not a whole-result undef; pin, libraries observe both the shape and the warning count.
Unary minus: -[1,[2,-3]] == [-1,[-2,3]]; -undef -> undef; -"a" -> undef + warning.
Ranges and strings as operands -> undef + warning (ranges do not behave as vectors in arithmetic).
Booleans as elements or operands -> undef (that element/operation) + warning.
undef operand -> undef (VERIFY whether an additional warning fires or the earlier undef's warning suffices).
nan/inf elements flow through elementwise arithmetic by IEEE rules with no extra warnings.
Every warning counts under --hardwarnings; the warning SET is compatibility surface.
impl_notes: Oracle-probe the mismatch matrix (scalar+vec, len mismatch, nested mismatch, string/bool/range/undef elements) recording BOTH the value shape and the exact warning lines/counts. Do not add broadcasting as an extension default — it changes undef-propagation behavior real scripts test for.

name: * operator: dot product and matrix multiplication
signature: a * b  — shape-dispatched: scalar*scalar | scalar*vector | vector*vector (DOT) | matrix*vector | vector*matrix | matrix*matrix
summary: Multiplication dispatches on operand shape: scalars scale vectors elementwise (recursively), flat-vector*flat-vector is a DOT PRODUCT (scalar result — not elementwise!), and nested row-major lists multiply as matrices.
semantics: Dispatch rules: number*number is a product. number*vector (either order) scales elementwise, recursing into nesting, so scalar*matrix works. vector*vector where both are flat numeric vectors of equal length is the dot product, returning a SCALAR. When vectors contain vector elements they are treated as row-major matrices: matrix*vector returns the vector of row dot products (length = row count); vector*matrix returns the vector of column dot products (length = column count, requires len(v) == row count of the matrix); matrix*matrix is the standard product over matching inner dimensions. Any dimension mismatch or non-numeric content yields undef with a WARNING. There is NO elementwise vector*vector multiply anywhere — users write comprehensions. Division: vector/scalar divides elementwise recursively; every other vector division form is undefined.
edge_cases: [1,2,3]*[4,5,6] == 32 — DOT PRODUCT, a scalar; newcomers expecting elementwise [4,10,18] must not get it.
Dot with unequal lengths -> undef + WARNING.
Matrix*vector: [[1,0],[0,2]]*[3,4] == [3,8]; requires every row length == len(v), else undef + warning. Vector*matrix: [3,4]*[[1,0],[0,2]] == [3,8] (column dots); requires len(v) == number of rows.
Matrix*matrix: [[1,2]]*[[3],[4]] == [[11]] (1x2 by 2x1); inner-dimension mismatch -> undef + warning.
VERIFY: ragged matrices (rows of differing lengths) — believed whole-result undef + warning, not partial results; pin.
VERIFY: [] * [] and M * [] — believed undef (+ warning); candidate alternative for empty dot is 0; pin against oracle.
Non-numeric element anywhere in a dot/matrix operand -> VERIFY whole-result undef vs nan-propagation; strings/bools/undef as operands -> undef + warning.

Vectors of vectors of vectors (3+ deep) are not tensors: dispatch only distinguishes 'elements are vectors' vs not — VERIFY exact behavior on depth-3 operands (believed treated as matrices whose 'scalars' are vectors, producing elementwise-recursive adds inside dots — pin, multmatrix-adjacent code hits it).
2/[1,2] is defined: elementwise scalar-by-vector division yields [2, 1]; see the / entry. Only vector/vector division is undef.
Dot/matrix results use IEEE double accumulation in element order — VERIFY summation order if bit-exact echo parity of large dots is desired.
Same row-major nested-list convention as multmatrix(m); precedence of * over +/- is ordinary.
impl_notes: Implement dispatch by runtime shape inspection (is-vector of first element), matching OpenSCAD's observable choices; oracle-probe the full mismatch matrix including empty operands, ragged rows, depth-3 nesting, and scalar/vector division forms, capturing warning text. Left-to-right accumulation preserves echo-level determinism.

name: echo
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
summary: Prints one console line 'ECHO: ...' at instantiation/evaluation time; the expression form additionally evaluates to its trailing expression, enabling tracing inside functions.

params.name: arg, ...
params.desc: Positional values of any type, printed in order joined by ', ' using the shared value formatter (strings quoted, numbers 6-sig-digit %g, vectors recursive).

params.name: name=value, ...
params.desc: Named arguments print as 'name = value', interleaved with positionals in written order. $-prefixed named arguments are NOT printed — they set special variables instead (VERIFY).

semantics: Module/statement form: echo(...) emits exactly one line, 'ECHO: ' followed by the rendered arguments joined by ', '. Emission happens during tree instantiation, depth-first, in source order — before and independent of geometry evaluation, and NOT suppressed by geometry caching (a module instantiated 100 times echoes 100 times). Expression form (2019.05): 'echo(args) expr' prints the line, then evaluates and yields expr; it prints on EVERY evaluation, making it the only tracing tool inside functions and comprehensions; echo-expressions chain and nest with let/assert expressions.
edge_cases: Rendering: strings quoted at top level (echo("hi") -> ECHO: "hi") — the deliberate asymmetry with str(); numbers exactly as str() (6 significant digits, 1234567 -> 1.23457e+6, inf/nan); vectors [a, b, c] with interior strings quoted; booleans true/false; undef prints undef; ranges spaced-colon form (VERIFY implicit step display); function literals as source-like text (VERIFY exact).
VERIFY: interior quotes/backslashes in printed strings are NOT re-escaped (echo("a\"b") believed 'ECHO: "a"b"').
Named args: echo(b=2) -> 'ECHO: b = 2' (spaces around =); mixed echo(1, x=2, 3) preserves written order (VERIFY ordering).
VERIFY: echo() with no arguments prints bare 'ECHO: ' (trailing space presence — pin exactly for golden tests).
VERIFY: $-named args are consumed as special-variable settings, not printed: echo($fn=5) believed to print 'ECHO: ' with nothing (pin).

Expression form with no trailing expression is a parse error; the form binds tightly: x = echo("trace") compute(y); is the idiom; prints once per EVALUATION, so inside a recursive function it prints per call — recursion tracing works.
VERIFY: children given to the module form (echo("x") cube();) — believed accepted and IGNORED silently in 2021.01 (pin; some snapshots warn that echo does not support children).

Timing/order: echoes appear in depth-first instantiation order, interleaved with WARNINGs; all echoes precede rendering output; re-compiles (F5 then F6, or each animation frame) re-emit everything; CLI writes ECHO lines to the console (VERIFY stderr-vs-stdout) or to a file with -o out.echo — the .echo export is the golden-test oracle format.
Rate limiting of duplicate lines is GUI console behavior only, not language semantics — the CLI/.echo stream contains every line.
No return value in module form; in expression form the echo itself has no value — only the trailing expression's value passes through.
example: echo("v=", [1,"a"], x=42); function f(n) = echo("n is", n) n*2; y = f(3);
impl_notes: Route all output through the shared str/echo formatter. Support -o file.echo equivalent early — it is the single most useful differential-testing channel against the official binary. Pin: zero-arg output, $-arg swallowing, child handling, stream (stderr), and quoting of embedded quotes.

name: assert
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
signature: assert(condition);  assert(condition, message);   |   assert(condition, message) expression   (expression form 2019.05+)
summary: Halts evaluation with a formatted ERROR plus TRACE stack when the condition is falsy; the expression form otherwise yields its trailing expression. The only throwing construct in the language.

params.name: condition
params.desc: Any value, tested with standard truthiness: exactly the five falsy values — false, 0 (and -0), "", [], undef — FAIL; everything else passes, including nan (assert(0/0) passes), "false", [0], and -1; everything else (including "false", [0], -1) passes.

params.name: message
params.desc: Optional; any value, rendered with the echo value formatter and appended to the error line after ': '. VERIFY: evaluated eagerly with the call (believed) rather than only on failure.

semantics: On a truthy condition, the statement form does nothing (its children, if any, instantiate normally — VERIFY) and the expression form evaluates to its trailing expression. On a falsy condition, evaluation HALTS immediately with an ERROR line naming the re-serialized SOURCE TEXT of the condition expression, the optional message, and the file and line, followed by one 'TRACE:' line per frame of the module instantiation stack. Nothing renders; the CLI exits nonzero. Expression asserts chain: assert(a) assert(b) expr. Introduced 2019.05; the canonical argument-validation tool for libraries.
edge_cases: Failure output shape: ERROR: Assertion '(cond-source-text)' failed: "message" in file <path>, line <N> — then TRACE: called by '<module>', in file <path>, line <N> lines unwinding the module stack innermost-first. VERIFY every punctuation detail verbatim (quoting of the condition, parentheses, message quoting, comma placement) — users and CI parse it.

The condition text is the AST re-serialization, not verbatim source: normalized whitespace and possibly added parentheses (assert(1+1==3) may render as '((1 + 1) == 3)') — VERIFY exact serializer output on a probe battery.
Message rendered like an echo VALUE: string messages believed printed WITH quotes; non-string messages (numbers, vectors) render in display form; omitted message omits the ': msg' segment entirely.
Truthiness traps: assert([]) FAILS (empty vector falsy); assert("false") PASSES; assert(0/0) PASSES (nan is truthy — toBool is a plain != 0 test); assert(undef) fails.

Expression form: assert(cond, msg) expr — lazy only in the sense that expr is unreached on failure; chains and mixes with let/echo expressions; inside functions a failure reports the assert's own file/line with the MODULE instantiation TRACE (VERIFY whether intermediate function call sites appear — believed not, modules only).
VERIFY: statement-form assert with a child (assert(x) cube();) — believed the child instantiates normally on success; pin.
VERIFY: assert() with no arguments and assert(a, b, extra) — pin the too-few/too-many argument warnings/errors.
Halting is total: no further echoes, warnings, or geometry from anywhere in the tree after the failure (VERIFY whether top-level statements after the failing one are reached — believed not).
Pre-2019.05 compatibility: on 2015.03 assert is an unknown module (warned, ignored) / unknown function — version-gate via version_num.
Not affected by --hardwarnings (already fatal); assert is the ONLY user-reachable hard stop besides syntax/recursion errors.
example: module ring(r) { assert(r > 0, "radius must be positive"); circle(r); } ring(5);
impl_notes: Implement an AST-to-source serializer for the condition text and freeze it against oracle probes (operators, calls, indexing, ternaries). Halt via an evaluator-level exception that still flushes prior console output in order. Exit code and stderr formatting are part of the CLI contract.

name: version
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
signature: version() -> [year, month] (release builds) | [year, month, day] (date-versioned snapshots)
summary: Returns the OpenSCAD version as a numeric vector, e.g. [2021, 1]; the vector-shaped twin of version_num().
semantics: Returns a vector of numbers identifying the running interpreter (two elements on release builds, three on date-versioned snapshot builds): [2021, 1] for release 2021.01. Libraries use it (usually via version_num instead, since vectors don't compare with <) to feature-gate code paths.
edge_cases: Dev snapshots report their snapshot date: believed [YYYY, M, D] (e.g. a 2025-02-19 nightly -> [2025, 2, 19]) — VERIFY mapping.

Elements are plain numbers; the vector itself cannot be relationally compared (version() > [2019,5,0] is undef!) — code must index elements or use version_num; a reimplementation must NOT make vector comparison work to 'help'.
VERIFY: arguments passed to version() — believed ignored, possibly with an unused-argument warning; pin.

What a reimplementation reports is a policy decision with real consequences: report [2021, 1] to unlock 2021.01 codepaths in BOSL2 etc.; reporting a fake future date may enable snapshot-only paths that then fail.

Release versions are two-element vectors: version() == [2021, 1] on the 2021.01 release, so version()[2] is undef and len(version()) == 2. A third (day) element appears only on date-versioned snapshot builds. version_num() is unaffected: the missing day fills as 0, giving 20210100.
impl_notes: Report [2021, 1] for a 2021.01-compat mode; if the app exposes opt-in snapshot features, still consider keeping version() at the compat baseline and documenting the choice — libraries key behavior off it.

name: version_num
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
summary: Returns the version as a single comparable number, e.g. 20210100 for release 2021.01 — the standard feature-test value.
semantics: Encodes the version as YYYYMMPP: year * 10000 + month * 100 + patch. Release 2021.01 returns 20210100. Because it is a plain number it works with relational operators, making it the idiomatic feature gate: if (version_num() >= 20190500) use 2019.05 features.
edge_cases: Dev snapshots: believed YYYYMMDD of the snapshot date (e.g. 20250219) — which makes snapshot values numerically interleave oddly with release+patch encoding; VERIFY mapping before mimicking snapshots.

Returns a double like every OpenSCAD number; 6-significant-digit echo formatting renders it in scientific notation (echo(version_num()) -> 2.02101e+7) — the VALUE is exact even though the echo text is rounded; feature tests compare the value, not the text.
VERIFY: arguments ignored / warned.
Real-world gates to satisfy: >= 20150300 (concat/chr/text era), >= 20190500 (assert/ord/each era), >= 20210100 (function literals/^). Whatever you report toggles those library branches.
impl_notes: Keep version() and version_num() consistent with each other. Report 20210100 in compat mode. Document that echo's scientific rendering of the value is expected and correct.

name: parent_module
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
signature: parent_module(n) -> string  (module name n levels up the instantiation stack)
summary: Introspects the dynamic module instantiation stack by name; with $parent_modules it enables the classic echo-driven BOM pattern.

params.name: n
params.desc: Stack depth to look up: 0 is the currently executing module, 1 its instantiating parent, and so on. Valid range is [0, $parent_modules - 1].

semantics: Returns the NAME (a string) of the module n levels above the current point in the dynamic instantiation stack — the stack of module calls that led to the current instantiation, not the lexical nesting. The canonical use is bill-of-materials generation: a part module echoes str("part used by: ", parent_module(1)), or walks the whole stack with for (i = [0 : $parent_modules - 1]).
edge_cases: VERIFY: parent_module(0) returns the CURRENT module's own name (believed; pin the zero-point convention — off-by-one here silently breaks BOM scripts).

Out-of-range n (>= $parent_modules, or any call at top level where the stack is empty): believed an ERROR approximately 'Parent module index (n) out of range' — VERIFY exact text and whether it hard-stops or warns and yields undef.
VERIFY: negative or fractional n — pin truncation vs error.
The stack is DYNAMIC: the same module reports different parents depending on call path; for-loops, if-blocks and anonymous braces do not push named frames.
VERIFY: whether built-in module instantiations (translate, union, ...) appear as frames or only user-defined modules — pin, it changes every reported depth/name.
Functions do not push module frames: calling parent_module inside a function reflects the module context the function was called from (VERIFY).

children() re-instantiation: children evaluate with the instantiating site's dynamic context — VERIFY which stack a child's parent_module sees (believed the stack at the children() call, i.e. including the callee module).
Interacts with the geometry cache: echo-based BOM output re-emits per instantiation regardless of caching (echoes are not cached away).
Returns a plain string comparable with == for dispatch-on-caller tricks (real scripts do this).
example: module part() { echo(str("part called by: ", parent_module(1))); cube(1); } module asm() part(); asm();
impl_notes: Maintain an explicit instantiation-stack of module names in the evaluator (needed anyway for TRACE output and recursion detection). Oracle-pin: the index-0 convention, out-of-range message, and whether builtin modules count as frames — the three highest-risk details.

name: $parent_modules
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
summary: The depth of the module instantiation stack at the point of evaluation; the loop bound for parent_module(n).
semantics: A dynamically scoped special variable holding how many module frames are on the instantiation stack. At the top level it is 0; inside a user module called from the top level it is 1 (VERIFY the exact counting origin together with parent_module's index-0 convention — the two must stay consistent: valid parent_module indices are [0, $parent_modules - 1]).
edge_cases: VERIFY: top-level value is 0 and each user-module instantiation increments by 1; pin whether builtin modules increment (must match parent_module's frame rule).
Like all $-variables it is readable anywhere, including inside functions, reflecting the dynamic call context.

VERIFY: assigning to it ($parent_modules = 5;) — believed a legal but meaningless shadow that the engine's own reads ignore or that actually shadows for descendants; pin (same question applies to $children).

Canonical idiom: for (i = [0 : $parent_modules - 1]) echo(parent_module(i)); — note that at depth 0 this range is [0 : -1], which under 2021.01's legacy range-swap rules DEPRECATION-warns and iterates — real BOM scripts guard with if ($parent_modules > 0).
example: module a() b(); module b() echo(depth = $parent_modules); a();
impl_notes: Derive from the same evaluator stack as parent_module and TRACE; never store independently. Pin counting origin via oracle before freezing.

name: rands
category: Other builtins: echo, assert, version, introspection
signature: rands(min_value, max_value, value_count, seed_value = undef) -> vector of numbers
summary: Vector of uniformly distributed random doubles; deterministic per call when seeded; ALWAYS returns a vector, even for a single value.

params.name: min_value
params.desc: Lower bound of the uniform range.

params.name: max_value
params.desc: Upper bound of the uniform range.

params.name: value_count
params.desc: How many values to generate. 0 yields [].

params.name: seed_value
params.desc: Optional numeric seed. When given, the call uses a FRESH generator seeded with it, so identical seeded calls return identical vectors. When omitted, values come from a shared nondeterministic stream.

semantics: Returns a vector of value_count doubles uniformly distributed over [min_value, max_value]. With a seed, results are reproducible: the same (min, max, count, seed) always yields the same vector within a given OpenSCAD build, and two identical seeded calls in one script are identical to each other (each seeded call re-seeds a fresh generator). Without a seed, each call draws from a global stream seeded unpredictably, differing between runs and between preview/render compiles.
edge_cases: ALWAYS a vector: rands(0,1,1) == [x] (single-element vector — scripts index [0]); rands(0,1,0) == [].
VERIFY: negative value_count — believed [] plus a WARNING (approx 'rands() cannot create a negative number of random values'); fractional counts believed truncated toward zero; pin both.
min_value == max_value -> every element exactly that value.
VERIFY: min > max — believed the bounds are swapped (or C++-UB territory in the official build); pin actual output and whether a warning fires.
VERIFY: endpoint inclusivity — documented as inclusive [min, max], but std::uniform_real_distribution is [min, max); observable only statistically, document as [min, max) reachable-in-practice.
undef/nan/inf bounds or count: VERIFY — believed undef result or nan-filled vector with conversion warning; pin each combination.
Seed handling: VERIFY fractional seeds (4 vs 4.5 — believed distinct via internal conversion, but pin truncation/collision behavior), negative seeds, and seed 0 vs unseeded distinction.

Seeded reproducibility holds within one OpenSCAD version/build only: the PRNG is std::mt19937 fed through the C++ STANDARD-LIBRARY-SPECIFIC uniform_real_distribution — official Windows/Mac/Linux builds may already differ from each other (VERIFY), and pre-2015 versions used a different RNG entirely.
Unseeded randomness re-rolls on every compile: preview then render produce different geometry — a known user gotcha; seeded calls are stable across F5/F6.

rands drives no geometry caching exemption: two instantiations of a module containing unseeded rands produce different values (module bodies re-evaluate; only geometry results are cached — VERIFY the interaction: identical subtrees with unseeded rands and whether cache collapses them).
impl_notes: Promise seeded self-determinism (same seed -> same vector in YOUR implementation), and explicitly DO NOT promise bit-compatibility with OpenSCAD's sequences — that would require cloning std::mt19937 plus a specific stdlib's uniform_real_distribution, and the official builds may not even agree cross-platform. Oracle probes: negative/fractional counts, swapped bounds, fractional seeds, warning texts.
since: pre-2015.03 (RNG algorithm changed across early versions — VERIFY which release fixed the current mt19937 behavior)

name: $fn
summary: Fragment-count override for circle tessellation: when > 0 it forces the exact number of fragments for a full circle, bypassing $fa/$fs entirely.

params.name: value
params.desc: Number of fragments for a full 360-degree circle. 0 (default) means 'use $fa/$fs formula'. Values 1 and 2 are raised to the minimum of 3.

semantics: Dynamically scoped like all $-variables. Read by every consumer of the fragment formula: circle(), sphere() (meridian count; latitude rings = ceil(N/2)), cylinder() (fragments from max(r1,r2)), rotate_extrude() (scaled by angle/360), offset(r=...), text() glyph-outline flattening, and the default slices computation of linear_extrude() with twist. When $fn > 0 the fragment count is max(int($fn), 3) and $fa/$fs are ignored completely. Can be set at any scope level, per-call as a named argument (sphere(10, $fn=64)), via let($fn=...), or injected with -D '$fn=64'.
edge_cases: Full fragment formula (documented in the manual): if r < GRID_FINE (2^-20 ~= 9.5367e-7) -> 3 fragments regardless of everything else; else if $fn > 0 -> max($fn,3) as integer; else -> ceil(max(min(360/$fa, 2*PI*r/$fs), 5)).
VERIFY: fractional $fn is truncated toward zero when cast to int (e.g. $fn=4.9 -> 4 fragments), not rounded or ceiled — pin via oracle.
$fn=1 and $fn=2 silently become 3 fragments; no warning is emitted.

Negative $fn fails the '> 0' test and falls through to the $fa/$fs path (it is NOT clamped to 3). NaN or +/-inf $fn instead short-circuits to exactly 3 fragments (it shares the tiny-radius branch, tested BEFORE $fn > 0).
$fn=0 is the documented way to re-enable $fa/$fs after a coarser scope set $fn.
Very large $fn (e.g. 1000) emits no warning; it just produces huge meshes. Performance behavior is user-visible.
$fn set as a call argument affects the whole subtree of that call (dynamic scoping), including children() re-instantiations under a module.
sphere($fn=6) yields 6 meridians and ceil(6/2)=3 latitude rings at half-step phase offsets — no pole vertices; models depend on this exact shape.
circle first vertex at angle 0 on +X, CCW winding, polygon INSCRIBED — $fn=6 hex-nut idiom and r/cos(180/n) compensation must keep working.
$fn is not consumed by cube/square/polygon/polyhedron; passing it there is harmless (all $-args are always accepted).
VERIFY: rotate_extrude with $fn and partial angle uses max(ceil($fn * angle/360), 1) fragments for the sweep — pin exact rounding.
VERIFY: text() maps $fn to bezier-flattening segment count of glyph outlines; exact mapping (segments per full turn vs per curve) must be pinned via oracle.
impl_notes: Pin the exact formula (including the GRID_FINE=2^-20 tiny-radius short-circuit, int truncation of $fn, and the floor of 3) with oracle probes: echo-free geometry probes via .csg/STL vertex counts at $fn in {0,1,2,2.5,4.9,6}. Fragment count feeds mesh topology, so a one-off here breaks every golden mesh test.

name: $fa
